interview.subject: System Design
interview.title: Functional & Non-Functional Requirements
interview.deck: Before you draw a single box or arrow, you must know what you're building and how well it needs to work — this lesson teaches you the very first step of every system design interview.
interview.oneIdea: Every system design starts with a single question: "What should this system do, and how well should it do it?" The answer splits into two clean buckets:

interview.subject: System Design
interview.title: Serverless vs Serverful Architecture
interview.deck: There are still servers in "serverless" — you just don't manage them. Understanding when to hand control to the cloud vs keeping your own fleet is a critical system design skill.
interview.oneIdea: In serverful architecture, you provision, manage, and pay for servers whether they're busy or idle. In serverless , the cloud provider dynamically allocates compute per request — you write code, they run it, and you pay only for what you use. The trade-off is control vs convenience .

interview.oneIdea: When your system can't handle the load, you have exactly two options: Vertical Scaling (Scale Up) — get a bigger machine, or Horizontal Scaling (Scale Out) — get more machines. Vertical is simpler but has hard limits; horizontal is complex but scales infinitely. Almost every large-scale system ultim...

interview.subject: System Design
interview.title: SQL vs NoSQL Databases
interview.deck: The most frequent architectural decision you will make. Picking the wrong database paradigm will doom your system's scaling potential or cripple your data integrity.
interview.oneIdea: SQL (Relational) databases are built for strict schema, strong data integrity (ACID), and complex relationships via JOIN s, but they are historically hard to scale horizontally. NoSQL (Non-Relational) databases sacrifice complex querying and strict schemas to achieve extreme horizontal scalability, ...
interview.keyVisual:
TypeHow it stores dataExamplesBest Used For
Key-Value A hash map (dictionary). Unique key points to a blob of data. Redis, Memcached, DynamoDB Caching, session storage, shopping carts, leaderboards. Extreme read/write speed.
Document JSON/BSON objects. Each document can have a completely different structure. MongoDB, Couchbase Content management, user profiles, product catalogs. Great when schema changes rapidly.
Column-Family Stores data by columns rather than rows. Highly optimized for massive write throughput across distributed nodes. Cassandra, HBase Time-series data, IoT sensor data, massive logging (e.g., Discord messages, Netflix viewing history).

interview.subject: System Design
interview.title: Data Replication & Schema Migration
interview.deck: Making sure your data outlives a single server crash and evolves safely.
interview.oneIdea: Making sure your data outlives a single server crash and evolves safely.
interview.keyVisual:
Aspect Synchronous Asynchronous
How it works Leader waits for Follower to confirm it saved the data before responding "Success" to the client. Leader writes data locally, says "Success" to client, and sends data to Follower in the background.
Latency High. Client waits for network roundtrips to all sync replicas. Low. Client gets immediate response.
Durability Perfect. If Leader dies, Follower has 100% of the data. Risky. If Leader dies before background sync, recent writes are permanently lost.

interview.subject: System Design
interview.title: Data Partitioning
interview.deck: Splitting your massive dataset into manageable chunks.
interview.oneIdea: Splitting your massive dataset into manageable chunks.
interview.keyVisual:
Vertical Partitioning (Splitting by Columns) Horizontal Partitioning / Sharding (Splitting by Rows)
You split tables based on columns. For example, moving the heavy profile_picture_url and bio columns to a different server than the frequently accessed username and password columns. You split tables based on rows. E.g., Users with IDs 1 to 10,000 live on Server A. Users with IDs 10,001 to 20,000 live on Server B. Both servers have the exact same table structure (columns).
Pros: Easy to implement initially. Optimizes disk I/O because you aren't pulling heavy, unused columns into memory. Pros: Truly infinite scale. You can just keep adding servers as your user base grows.
Cons: Has a hard limit. Eventually, even the vertically sliced tables will get too many rows to fit on one machine. Cons: Extremely complex. Cross-partition joins are terribly slow or impossible. Application logic must route queries to the correct server.

interview.keyVisual:
Aspect Stateful Session Cookies Stateless JWT (JSON Web Token)
Where state lives On the server (Redis cluster or database table). Client receives a random session ID string. Entirely in the token payload carried by the client. Server stores zero session state.
Verification Cost Requires a database/Redis lookup on every single HTTP request across all microservices. $0$ database calls! Verified cryptographically in CPU memory via public key or secret signature.
Revocation / Logout Trivial: Delete the session key from Redis. User is instantly logged out everywhere. Hard: Once issued, a JWT is valid until its expiration timestamp unless you maintain a revocation blacklist.

public class FenwickTree {
    private final int[] tree;

    public FenwickTree(int size) {
        this.tree = new int[size + 1]; // 1-based indexing
    }

    public void add(int i, int delta) {
        for (; i < tree.length; i += i & (-i)) {
            tree[i] += delta;
        }
    }

    public int queryPrefix(int i) {
        int sum = 0;
        for (; i > 0; i -= i & (-i)) {
            sum += tree[i];
        }
        return sum;
    }

    public int queryRange(int l, int r) {
        return queryPrefix(r) - queryPrefix(l - 1);
    }
}

public class CustomArrayList<T> {
    private Object[] data;
    private int size = 0;
    private static final int DEFAULT_CAPACITY = 10;

    public CustomArrayList() {
        this.data = new Object[DEFAULT_CAPACITY];
    }

    public void add(T element) {
        if (size == data.length) {
            resize(data.length * 2); // Geometric doubling
        }
        data[size++] = element;
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    public T get(int index) {
        if (index < 0 || index >= size) throw new IndexOutOfBoundsException();
        return (T) data[index]; // O(1) direct offset access
    }

    private void resize(int newCapacity) {
        Object[] newArray = new Object[newCapacity];
        System.arraycopy(data, 0, newArray, 0, size);
        this.data = newArray;
    }

    public int size() { return size; }
}

interview.title: Dutch National Flag & 3-Way Partitioning
interview.deck: Edsger Dijkstra's optimal one-pass in-place partitioning algorithm for three distinct categories.
interview.oneIdea: Given an array containing only 0s, 1s, and 2s (e.g. [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0] ), sort it in-place in a single pass without using extra counting arrays or library sort. Dijkstra's Dutch National Flag Algorithm divides the array into four zones using three pointers: low , mid , and high .
interview.keyVisual:
public class DutchNationalFlag {
    public static void sortColors(int[] nums) {
        int low = 0;
        int mid = 0;
        int high = nums.length - 1;

        while (mid <= high) {
            if (nums[mid] == 0) {
                swap(nums, low, mid);
                low++;
                mid++;
            } else if (nums[mid] == 1) {
                mid++; // 1 is already in its correct zone
            } else { // nums[mid] == 2
                swap(nums, mid, high);
                high--; // Do NOT increment mid; swapped element is unexamined!
            }
        }
    }

    private static void swap(int[] arr, int i, int j) {
        int temp = arr[i];
        arr[i] = arr[j];
        arr[j] = temp;
    }
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: String Matching: KMP & Rabin-Karp
interview.deck: Linear-time substring search without backtracking using deterministic preprocessing.
interview.oneIdea: To check if pattern $P$ (length $M$) exists in text $T$ (length $N$), naive brute force compares character by character, resetting back to index 0 on mismatch ($O(N \cdot M)$ worst case). The Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm precomputes an auxiliary LPS (Longest Proper Prefix which is also a Suffi...
interview.keyVisual:
public class KMPAlgorithm {
    public static int[] computeLPS(String pattern) {
        int m = pattern.length();
        int[] lps = new int[m];
        int len = 0; // Length of previous longest prefix suffix
        int i = 1;

        while (i < m) {
            if (pattern.charAt(i) == pattern.charAt(len)) {
                len++;
                lps[i] = len;
                i++;
            } else {
                if (len != 0) {
                    len = lps[len - 1]; // Fall back to shorter prefix
                } else {
                    lps[i] = 0;
                    i++;
                }
            }
        }
        return lps;
    }

    public static int search(String text, String pattern) {
        int[] lps = computeLPS(pattern);
        int i = 0, j = 0;

        while (i < text.length()) {
            if (pattern.charAt(j) == text.charAt(i)) {
                i++;
                j++;
            }
            if (j == pattern.length()) {
                return i - j; // Found match at index!
            } else if (i < text.length() && pattern.charAt(j) != text.charAt(i)) {
                if (j != 0) j = lps[j - 1];
                else i++;
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Choose → Explore → Unchoose
interview.deck: Backtracking is just DFS on an imaginary tree of decisions — one template, three lines of ritual, and it generates every subset, permutation, and combination you'll ever be asked for.
interview.oneIdea: You already know recursion. Backtracking is recursion with one twist: you build a partial candidate (a growing list called path ) as you recurse, and you undo each addition on the way back up so the same path object can be reused for the next branch. Picture a decision tree : the root is the empty c...
interview.keyVisual:
List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();

List<List<Integer>> subsets(int[] nums) {
    backtrack(nums, 0, new ArrayList<>());
    return res;
}

void backtrack(int[] nums, int start, List<Integer> path) {
    res.add(new ArrayList<>(path));       // record a COPY — every node of the tree is a subset
    for (int i = start; i < nums.length; i++) {
        path.add(nums[i]);                // CHOOSE: include nums[i]
        backtrack(nums, i + 1, path);     // EXPLORE: only indices AFTER i (no reordering, no reuse)
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);     // UNCHOOSE: undo, so the next i starts clean
    }
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Combination Sum & String Backtracking
interview.deck: Same choose→explore→unchoose skeleton, two new levers: a numeric budget that prunes branches, and strings where each "choice" is the next chunk you consume or the next character you append.
interview.oneIdea: Lesson 1's template enumerated structures (subsets, permutations). This lesson adds a goal and a budget : carry the remaining target down the tree, succeed when it hits 0, and prune any branch that already overshot. The single most-tested detail: when an element may be reused , recurse with i (stay ...
interview.keyVisual:
List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();

List<List<Integer>> combinationSum(int[] cand, int target) {
    Arrays.sort(cand);                    // enables the break-prune below
    backtrack(cand, 0, target, new ArrayList<>());
    return res;
}

void backtrack(int[] cand, int start, int remain, List<Integer> path) {
    if (remain == 0) {                    // budget exactly spent → record a leaf
        res.add(new ArrayList<>(path));
        return;
    }
    for (int i = start; i < cand.length; i++) {
        if (cand[i] > remain) break;      // PRUNE: sorted, so every later cand is too big too
        path.add(cand[i]);                // CHOOSE
        backtrack(cand, i, remain - cand[i], path); // EXPLORE with i (NOT i+1): reuse allowed
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);     // UNCHOOSE
    }
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Grid & Constraint Puzzles
interview.deck: When the state you mutate is the board itself: mark a cell, place a queen, pencil in a digit — explore — then erase. Plus the line between "TLE" and "accepted": pruning, and knowing when backtracking is secretly DP.
interview.oneIdea: So far path was a private list. In puzzles, the shared mutable state is the input structure itself : choose = write into the board (mark a visited cell, place a 'Q' , fill a digit), explore = recurse, unchoose = erase your write . Two upgrades make these pass instead of TLE: (1) check constraints be...
interview.keyVisual:
boolean exist(char[][] board, String word) {
    for (int r = 0; r < board.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < board[0].length; c++)
            if (dfs(board, word, r, c, 0)) return true;   // try every start cell
    return false;
}

boolean dfs(char[][] b, String w, int r, int c, int i) {
    if (i == w.length()) return true;     // consumed the whole word → found
    if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= b.length || c >= b[0].length
        || b[r][c] != w.charAt(i))        // out of bounds, wrong char, or '#' (visited)
        return false;
    char saved = b[r][c];
    b[r][c] = '#';                        // CHOOSE: mark in place — no separate visited[][]
    boolean found = dfs(b, w, r + 1, c, i + 1) || dfs(b, w, r - 1, c, i + 1)
                 || dfs(b, w, r, c + 1, i + 1) || dfs(b, w, r, c - 1, i + 1);
    b[r][c] = saved;                      // UNCHOOSE: ALWAYS restore, found or not
    return found;
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Binary Search as a Boundary Finder
interview.deck: Forget "find the target in a sorted array." Binary search finds the boundary where a monotonic yes/no question flips from NO to YES — and once you see it that way, every variant is the same six lines.
interview.oneIdea: Take any yes/no question p(i) over indices 0..n-1 that is monotonic : once it becomes true, it stays true. The answers look like F F F F T T T — a wall of falses, then a wall of trues. Binary search is the O(log n) way to find the first T . That's it. "Find 7 in a sorted array" is just the question ...
interview.keyVisual:
// Find the smallest i in [0, n] such that p(i) is true; returns n if p is never true.
int firstTrue(int n, IntPredicate p) {
    int lo = 0, hi = n;                  // answer lives in [lo, hi]; hi = n means "no true exists"
    while (lo < hi) {                    // stop when exactly one candidate remains
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;    // overflow-safe midpoint (see trap below)
        if (p.test(mid)) hi = mid;       // mid is true → first true is mid OR earlier → keep mid
        else lo = mid + 1;               // mid is false → first true is strictly after mid
    }
    return lo;                           // lo == hi == the boundary
}

// lowerBound: first index with nums[i] >= target — the workhorse instance of firstTrue.
int lowerBound(int[] nums, int target) {
    int lo = 0, hi = nums.length;
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] >= target) hi = mid;
        else lo = mid + 1;
    }
    return lo;                           // may be nums.length → target > everything
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Rotated & Modified Binary Search
interview.deck: Rotated arrays, peaks, and 2D matrices aren't sorted — but at every midpoint you can still answer "which side is the target on?" in O(1). That question is all binary search ever needed.
interview.oneIdea: Lesson 1 needed a monotonic predicate. These arrays aren't monotonic — a rotated array goes up, cliffs down, goes up again. But binary search never needed sorted ; it needed: at each mid, decide in O(1) which half can't contain the answer, and throw it away. In a rotated array, one half of any split...
interview.keyVisual:
// LC 153: min of a rotated sorted array with DISTINCT values.
int findMin(int[] nums) {
    int lo = 0, hi = nums.length - 1;    // nums[hi] is the anchor; answer guaranteed in [lo, hi]
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
        if (nums[mid] <= nums[hi]) hi = mid; // mid is in the right sorted run → min is mid or left of it
        else lo = mid + 1;               // mid in left run (> nums[hi]) → min is strictly right
    }
    return nums[lo];                     // lo = first index of the right run = the minimum
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Binary Search on the Answer
interview.deck: When you can't compute the answer but you CAN check a guess — "could Koko finish at speed 6?" — binary search the guesses. This is the single most common pattern in big-tech online assessments.
interview.oneIdea: Stop searching the input. Search the space of possible answers . If Koko can finish the bananas eating at speed 6, she can certainly finish at 7, 8, 9… — feasibility is monotonic in the guess : F F F T T T over speeds. So write a checker feasible(guess) (usually a greedy O(n) simulation), and run Le...
interview.keyVisual:
// Minimize x in [lo, hi] such that feasible(x) — feasible must be monotonic F…FT…T.
int minFeasible(int lo, int hi) {         // pick lo/hi so the answer is GUARANTEED inside
    while (lo < hi) {
        int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;     // ranges hit 10⁹ here — the overflow guard earns its keep
        if (feasible(mid)) hi = mid;      // mid works → try smaller, but keep mid
        else lo = mid + 1;                // mid fails → everything ≤ mid fails too
    }
    return lo;
}

boolean feasible(int x) {                 // the ONLY problem-specific part: an O(n) greedy check
    // "if the answer were x, could we do the task?" — simulate and compare to the budget
    return true;
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Bit Manipulation — Operators & Tricks
interview.deck: An int is 32 switches. Learn the six operators and a handful of one-line tricks, and a whole category of OA questions becomes free points.
interview.oneIdea: A Java int is a row of 32 bits — treat it as a set of 32 booleans you can read, flip, and combine in a single CPU instruction. Everything in this track reduces to three moves: build a mask ( 1 << i ) to talk about bit i , combine masks with & | ^ , and exploit two magic identities — x &amp...
interview.keyVisual:
// ---- the two magic identities ----
x & (x - 1)        // CLEAR lowest set bit:  0b10110 → 0b10100
x & -x             // ISOLATE lowest set bit: 0b10110 → 0b00010

// ---- talk to bit i via the mask (1 << i) ----
(x >> i & 1) == 1  // GET   bit i (or: (x & (1 << i)) != 0 — never == 1!)
x | (1 << i)       // SET   bit i to 1
x & ~(1 << i)      // CLEAR bit i to 0
x ^ (1 << i)       // TOGGLE bit i

// ---- ready-made masks ----
(1 << k) - 1       // lowest k bits all 1:  k=4 → 0b1111
x & ((1 << k) - 1) // keep only the lowest k bits of x

// ---- instant checks ----
(x & 1) == 1                    // odd?
x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0     // power of two? (exactly one set bit)

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: XOR & Masks
interview.deck: One operator that makes duplicates annihilate each other, and one loop that enumerates every subset of a set — the two ideas behind a shelf of "impossible without the trick" problems.
interview.oneIdea: XOR is addition without carrying — per bit, "are they different?". Two properties do all the work: self-inverse ( a ^ a = 0 , and a ^ 0 = a ) and order-free (commutative + associative). XOR a whole array and you can mentally reorder it so every duplicate pair sits together and vanishes — whatever ap...
interview.keyVisual:
int singleNumber(int[] nums) {
    int x = 0;                 // 0 is XOR's identity
    for (int v : nums) x ^= v; // pairs annihilate (a ^ a = 0), order irrelevant
    return x;                  // the survivor: the one element with odd count
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Cyclic Sort
interview.deck: When an array of n numbers only contains values from 1 to n, each value has exactly one home: index value−1. Swap everything home in O(n), and the missing and duplicate numbers expose themselves.
interview.oneIdea: How do you find the missing number in an array? Naive: sort it, O(n log n), then scan. Or dump everything into a HashSet, O(n) time but O(n) space. Cyclic sort gets O(n) time and O(1) space by exploiting one fact the general-purpose tools ignore: the values are index-sized . If every value is in [1....
interview.keyVisual:
// Cyclic sort: values 1..n, each belongs at index value-1.
void cyclicSort(int[] a) {
    int i = 0;
    while (i < a.length) {
        int home = a[i] - 1;             // where the value under the finger belongs
        if (a[i] != a[home]) {           // not home yet (and home doesn't already hold a copy)
            int t = a[i]; a[i] = a[home]; a[home] = t; // send it home; inspect the newcomer next
        } else {
            i++;                         // a[i] is home (or its home is occupied by its twin) → move on
        }
    }
}                                        // afterwards: a[i] == i+1 wherever possible

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find) Mastery
interview.deck: Tracking connected components in nearly O(1) time using path compression and union by rank.
interview.oneIdea: Given a network of computers or friends, how do you determine whether two nodes belong to the same connected group, or dynamically add connections between groups? BFS/DFS takes $O(V + E)$ per query. Disjoint Set Union (DSU) maintains partition sets supporting two operations: find(x) (find the leader...
interview.keyVisual:
public class DisjointSetUnion {
    private final int[] parent;
    private final int[] rank;
    private int components;

    public DisjointSetUnion(int n) {
        this.parent = new int[n];
        this.rank = new int[n];
        this.components = n;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) parent[i] = i; // Self-parent initially
    }

    public int find(int i) {
        if (parent[i] == i) return i;
        return parent[i] = find(parent[i]); // Path Compression
    }

    public boolean union(int i, int j) {
        int rootI = find(i);
        int rootJ = find(j);
        if (rootI == rootJ) return false; // Already connected (Cycle detected!)

        // Union by rank
        if (rank[rootI] < rank[rootJ]) {
            parent[rootI] = rootJ;
        } else if (rank[rootI] > rank[rootJ]) {
            parent[rootJ] = rootI;
        } else {
            parent[rootJ] = rootI;
            rank[rootI]++;
        }
        components--;
        return true;
    }

    public int getComponents() { return components; }
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: DP Foundations
interview.deck: Dynamic programming is not a topic — it's one trick: never solve the same subproblem twice . Learn the 5-step framework here; every later lesson is that framework with a different state.
interview.oneIdea: DP = recursion + never solving the same subproblem twice . A problem is DP-shaped when it has overlapping subproblems (the naive recursion recomputes identical calls — fib(3) gets computed twice inside fib(5) ) and optimal substructure (the best answer to the whole is built from best answers to the ...
interview.keyVisual:
// The recursion tree doubles every level. fib(50) ≈ 10^10 calls — hangs forever.
int fib(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);   // fib(n-2) recomputes everything fib(n-1) already did
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: 1D DP on Sequences
interview.deck: One array in, one dp array over it. House Robber is the template; eight classic problems are that template with one twist each.
interview.oneIdea: For a single array or string, define dp[i] = the best answer for the prefix ending at (or up to) index i . The recurrence pulls from O(1) earlier states — dp[i-1] , dp[i-2] — or occasionally all O(i) of them. Scan left→right once, and the giant space of subsets/decodings/subarrays collapses into n c...
interview.keyVisual:
// Full table first — see the state.
int rob(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    if (n == 1) return nums[0];
    int[] dp = new int[n];
    dp[0] = nums[0];
    dp[1] = Math.max(nums[0], nums[1]);
    for (int i = 2; i < n; i++)
        dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i - 1],              // skip house i
                         dp[i - 2] + nums[i]);   // rob house i → i-1 forbidden
    return dp[n - 1];
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Grid DP (2D paths)
interview.deck: A robot that only moves right/down is a DAG in disguise — and index order is its topological sort. No BFS, no queue: just two nested loops.
interview.oneIdea: In a grid where moves go right/down, dp[r][c] depends on a constant set of already-filled neighbors — usually top ( dp[r-1][c] ) and left ( dp[r][c-1] ). Grid DP is graph DP on a DAG whose edges point right and down, so row-major iteration IS a topological order : by the time you reach a cell, every...
interview.keyVisual:
// Bottom-up 2D — see the whole table.
int uniquePaths(int m, int n) {
    int[][] dp = new int[m][n];                  // dp[r][c] = paths from (0,0) to (r,c)
    for (int r = 0; r < m; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < n; c++)
            dp[r][c] = (r == 0 || c == 0) ? 1    // edges: only one straight-line way
                     : dp[r - 1][c] + dp[r][c - 1];
    return dp[m - 1][n - 1];
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Knapsack: 0/1, unbounded & the loop-order rule
interview.deck: Items + capacity is the most reusable DP shape in interviews. Master two loop rules — descending vs ascending, items-outer vs target-outer — and eight LC problems collapse into one template.
interview.oneIdea: You have items and a capacity (weight limit, target sum, amount). The state is "(items considered so far, capacity used)". 0/1 knapsack : each item usable at most once → in the 1D version, iterate capacity descending . Unbounded knapsack : items reusable → iterate capacity ascending . And when count...
interview.keyVisual:
// dp[i][c] = max value using the first i items within capacity c.
int knapsack(int[] w, int[] val, int W) {
    int n = w.length;
    int[][] dp = new int[n + 1][W + 1];      // row 0 and column 0 stay 0 — the base case
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
        for (int c = 0; c <= W; c++) {
            dp[i][c] = dp[i - 1][c];         // choice 1: skip item i-1
            if (c >= w[i - 1])               // choice 2: take it ONCE — read the PREVIOUS row
                dp[i][c] = Math.max(dp[i][c], dp[i - 1][c - w[i - 1]] + val[i - 1]);
        }
    return dp[n][W];
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Two-string DP: the LCS family
interview.deck: Longest Common Subsequence is not one problem — it's a template. Match → diagonal + 1; mismatch → best of skip-left / skip-up. Change what "match" and "skip" cost and you get Edit Distance, Distinct Subsequences, and regex matching.
interview.oneIdea: With two strings, the state is a pair of prefixes : dp[i][j] = answer for s1[0..i) vs s2[0..j) . Every transition asks one question — do the last characters s1[i-1] and s2[j-1] agree? Match: extend the diagonal, dp[i-1][j-1] . Mismatch: combine the "skip one character" neighbors dp[i-1][j] / dp[i][j...
interview.keyVisual:
int longestCommonSubsequence(String s1, String s2) {
    int m = s1.length(), n = s2.length();
    int[][] dp = new int[m + 1][n + 1];      // row 0 / col 0 = vs empty string = 0
    for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++)
        for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++)
            if (s1.charAt(i - 1) == s2.charAt(j - 1))
                dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1;                  // match → extend diagonal
            else
                dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);  // skip one last char
    return dp[m][n];
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Palindrome DP
interview.deck: A palindrome is a palindrome wrapped in a matching pair: s[i..j] is one iff s[i] == s[j] and s[i+1..j-1] is. That nesting gives you an O(n²) table over substrings (i, j) — and a free O(1)-space alternative: expand around centers.
interview.oneIdea: Palindromes have recursive structure from the outside in : peel the matching outer pair and a smaller palindrome remains. So the natural state is a substring (i, j) , and the table must be filled by increasing length — the inner substring (i+1, j-1) is strictly shorter, so it's already known. For su...
interview.keyVisual:
// isPal[i][j] = true iff s[i..j] is a palindrome. O(n²) time and space.
boolean[][] buildIsPal(String s) {
    int n = s.length();
    boolean[][] isPal = new boolean[n][n];
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) isPal[i][i] = true;          // length 1
    for (int len = 2; len <= n; len++)                       // inner substrings already done
        for (int i = 0; i + len - 1 < n; i++) {
            int j = i + len - 1;
            isPal[i][j] = s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j)
                       && (len == 2 || isPal[i + 1][j - 1]); // len 2 has an empty inside
        }
    return isPal;
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence & friends
interview.deck: Learn LIS twice — the honest O(n²) DP and the patience-sorting tails trick — then unlock a whole family of 2D problems with one move: sort one dimension, LIS the other .
interview.oneIdea: LIS has two canonical solutions and you need both . The DP view: dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ending exactly at index i — extend any earlier smaller element, O(n²). The fast view: keep an array tails where tails[k] = the smallest possible tail of any increasing subsequence of...
interview.keyVisual:
int lengthOfLIS(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] dp = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(dp, 1);                       // base case: each element alone = length 1
    int best = 1;
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < i; j++)
            if (nums[j] < nums[i])            // strictly increasing — the ONLY line variants change
                dp[i] = Math.max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1);
        best = Math.max(best, dp[i]);         // answer = max over ALL endings
    }
    return best;
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: State-machine DP
interview.deck: Every stock problem — and paint, fence, and wiggle problems too — is a tiny automaton: a handful of named states and the legal moves between them. Draw it first; the recurrence is just the arrows.
interview.oneIdea: At each index you are in one of a few named states — holding a stock , free to buy , in cooldown , last house painted red . The rules of the problem are edges between states, forming a small automaton. Then dp[i][state] = best value at index i while in that state , and each transition reads straight...
interview.keyVisual:
int maxProfit(int[] prices) {
    int hold = Integer.MIN_VALUE / 2;         // -∞: holding before buying is unreachable. /2 avoids overflow on +p
    int free = 0;                             // profit 0, holding nothing
    for (int p : prices) {
        int prevFree = free;                  // snapshot: both updates must read YESTERDAY's values
        free = Math.max(free, hold + p);      // rest, or sell today
        hold = Math.max(hold, prevFree - p);  // rest, or buy today
    }
    return free;                              // finish holding nothing
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Interval DP (& game DP)
interview.deck: When the state is a whole subarray i..j , the winning trick is to pick the last operation — the last balloon burst, the last cut — so the two sides stop interfering with each other.
interview.oneIdea: dp[i][j] = the answer for the subarray/substring i..j . The transition picks a split point k inside the interval — but here's the counter-intuitive move that makes it work: let k be the LAST operation performed , not the first. If the balloon at k is the last one burst in (i, j) , then while everyth...
interview.keyVisual:
int maxCoins(int[] nums) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int[] a = new int[n + 2];
    a[0] = a[n + 1] = 1;                          // virtual 1-balloons: bursting an edge balloon pays 1·x·y
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i + 1] = nums[i];

    int[][] dp = new int[n + 2][n + 2];           // dp[i][j] = max coins from the OPEN interval (i, j)
    for (int len = 2; len <= n + 1; len++)        // len = j - i; len 1 (adjacent) stays 0 = base case
        for (int i = 0; i + len <= n + 1; i++) {
            int j = i + len;
            for (int k = i + 1; k < j; k++)       // k = LAST balloon to burst inside (i, j)
                dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i][j],
                    dp[i][k] + a[i] * a[k] * a[j] + dp[k][j]);
        }                                         // when k pops last, its neighbors ARE a[i] and a[j]
    return dp[0][n + 1];
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: DP on Trees
interview.deck: No table to fill here — the recursion is the iteration order. Each node returns a tiny tuple summarizing its subtree, and the parent just combines.
interview.oneIdea: On arrays we filled dp[i] left→right because state i depended on earlier indices. On a tree, a node's answer depends on its children's answers — so the natural fill order is postorder DFS : solve both subtrees first, then combine at the parent. The state is (node, small enum) — e.g. "best if this no...
interview.keyVisual:
// LC 337 House Robber III — THE tree-DP template. State enum = {robbed, skipped}.
int rob(TreeNode root) {
    int[] r = dfs(root);
    return Math.max(r[0], r[1]);           // answer lives at the root: rob it or not
}
int[] dfs(TreeNode node) {                 // returns {rob, skip} for node's subtree
    if (node == null) return new int[]{0, 0};       // base case
    int[] L = dfs(node.left), R = dfs(node.right);  // postorder: children FIRST
    int rob  = node.val + L[1] + R[1];              // rob me → children forced to skip
    int skip = Math.max(L[0], L[1]) + Math.max(R[0], R[1]); // skip me → children choose freely
    return new int[]{rob, skip};
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Bitmask DP
interview.deck: When n ≤ ~20, every subset of your items fits in one integer — so "best answer for this subset" becomes a plain array lookup: dp[mask] .
interview.oneIdea: "Try every permutation" is n! — dead at n = 12. But the optimal way to finish usually depends only on which items are already used , not the order you used them in. Encode that set as an int ( bit i set ⇔ item i used ) and you collapse n! orderings into 2ⁿ states. The killer convenience: every prope...
interview.keyVisual:
// CHECK — is item i in the subset?
boolean in = ((mask >> i) & 1) == 1;     // or: (mask & (1 << i)) != 0 — NEVER == 1, the bit's value is 2^i
// SET — add item i (idempotent: safe if already present)
mask |= (1 << i);
// CLEAR — remove item i (idempotent: safe if already absent)
mask &= ~(1 << i);
// TOGGLE — flip item i (add if absent, remove if present; only use XOR to "remove" when you KNOW it's set)
mask ^= (1 << i);
// POPCOUNT — how many items chosen: a free progress counter (hardware instruction, O(1))
int size = Integer.bitCount(mask);
// ITERATE the set bits without scanning all n positions:
for (int m = mask; m != 0; m &= (m - 1)) {        // m &= m-1 strips the LOWEST set bit each round
    int i = Integer.numberOfTrailingZeros(m);      // index of that bit → "item i is in the subset"
}
int low  = mask & (-mask);               // isolate the lowest set bit as a mask (two's complement trick)
int full = (1 << n) - 1;                 // the "everything chosen" mask: n ones

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Digit DP & the DP Cheat Sheet
interview.deck: "How many integers ≤ N have property P?" — when N is 10¹⁸, you don't iterate numbers, you build their digits . Then: the one-page revision card for all twelve DP families.
interview.oneIdea: Every number ≤ N can be built digit by digit, left to right. At each position you're in one of two worlds: tight — every digit so far equals N's prefix, so this digit may go only up to N's digit — or free — you already dipped below N somewhere, so anything 0–9 is legal. Count recursively over (pos, ...
interview.keyVisual:
char[] s;
Integer[][] memo;                          // memo[pos][state] — for tight == false only

long countUpTo(long N) {                   // numbers in [0, N] whose digits satisfy the property
    s = Long.toString(N).toCharArray();
    memo = new Integer[s.length][STATES];
    return dfs(0, START, true);
}
int dfs(int pos, int state, boolean tight) {
    if (pos == s.length) return accept(state) ? 1 : 0;   // a full number is built — does it qualify?
    if (!tight && memo[pos][state] != null) return memo[pos][state];
    int limit = tight ? s[pos] - '0' : 9;  // glued to N? can't exceed N's digit here
    int total = 0;
    for (int d = 0; d <= limit; d++)
        total += dfs(pos + 1, next(state, d), tight && d == limit);  // stay tight only on the max digit
    if (!tight) memo[pos][state] = total;
    return total;
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Fast & Slow Pointers — Cycle Detection
interview.deck: Two runners on the same track: if it loops, the fast one must lap the slow one. Cycles, midpoints, and "does this sequence repeat?" — all in O(1) space.
interview.oneIdea: Run two pointers from the head: slow moves 1 step per tick, fast moves 2. In a straight list, fast hits null and you're done — no cycle. In a cyclic list, both eventually orbit the loop, and since fast gains on slow by exactly one node per tick , the gap between them shrinks 1, 0 — they must collide...
interview.keyVisual:
boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;       // both start at head
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) { // fast does the null-checking for both
        slow = slow.next;                    // tortoise: 1 step
        fast = fast.next.next;               // hare: 2 steps
        if (slow == fast) return true;       // collision ⇒ cycle (compare AFTER moving)
    }
    return false;                            // fast fell off the end ⇒ straight list
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Fast & Slow — Gap Tricks & Applications
interview.deck: The same two-pointer race, redeployed: an array that secretly contains a cycle, palindromes checked in O(1) space, and a fixed-gap trick that deletes the nth-from-end in one pass.
interview.oneIdea: Fast & slow is really about the gap two pointers maintain. A growing gap (speeds 1 and 2) detects cycles and finds midpoints. A fixed gap (same speed, head start of n) finds "nth from the end" in one pass. And the structure doesn't have to be a linked list: any deterministic "next" — including i...
interview.keyVisual:
int findDuplicate(int[] nums) {
    int slow = nums[0], fast = nums[nums[0]];    // take 1 and 2 steps from "node" 0
    while (slow != fast) {                       // phase 1: collide inside the cycle
        slow = nums[slow];                       // slow = slow.next
        fast = nums[nums[fast]];                 // fast = fast.next.next
    }
    slow = 0;                                    // phase 2: reset to head (index 0)
    while (slow != fast) {
        slow = nums[slow];                       // both at speed 1 now
        fast = nums[fast];
    }
    return slow;                                 // cycle entrance = the duplicated value
}

interview.title: Graph Foundations
interview.deck: Before you can DFS or BFS anything, you must build the graph. Master the adjacency-list build and every later lesson becomes bookkeeping.
interview.oneIdea: A graph is just nodes (vertices, V ) + connections (edges, E ) . Trees, grids, linked lists, "course prerequisites", "word ladders", "friend networks" — all graphs. 99% of interview problems never hand you a graph object: they hand you raw edges ( int[][] edges ) or an implicit structure (a grid, a ...
interview.keyVisual:
// Input: n nodes (0..n-1) and edges[i] = {u, v}. UNDIRECTED graph.
List<List<Integer>> buildAdj(int n, int[][] edges) {
    List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());  // one empty list PER node — don't skip this
    for (int[] e : edges) {
        adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]);
        adj.get(e[1]).add(e[0]);   // BOTH directions because undirected. Directed? delete this line.
    }
    return adj;
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Depth-First Search
interview.deck: One recursive idea — dive as deep as you can, then back out — solves connectivity, islands, all-paths, and both flavors of cycle detection. The variations are bookkeeping on top of one template.
interview.oneIdea: DFS commits to one neighbor, follows it as far as it goes, and only backtracks when it dead-ends — "deep before wide." Mechanically it's a visited set plus either the call stack (recursion) or an explicit Deque used as a stack. The visited set is what makes a graph DFS terminate where a tree DFS nee...
interview.keyVisual:
// recursive graph DFS — the move you build everything else on
void dfs(int node, List<List<Integer>> adj, boolean[] visited) {
    visited[node] = true;            // mark ON ENTRY, before recursing
    for (int nei : adj.get(node)) {
        if (!visited[nei])
            dfs(nei, adj, visited);  // go deep into this branch first
    }
}

// driver: handles a disconnected graph by launching from every unvisited node
int countComponents(int n, List<List<Integer>> adj) {
    boolean[] visited = new boolean[n];
    int components = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        if (!visited[i]) { components++; dfs(i, adj, visited); }
    return components;
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Breadth-First Search & Shortest Paths
interview.deck: A queue expands a frontier one distance-ring at a time. The first time it touches a node in an unweighted graph, it arrived by a shortest path — that single guarantee is the whole pattern.
interview.oneIdea: BFS pushes a source into a FIFO queue and expands outward: it finishes every node at distance d before touching any node at distance d+1 . Because nodes come out in non-decreasing distance order, the first arrival at any node in an unweighted graph is already a shortest path — no relaxation, no prio...
interview.keyVisual:
// graph BFS with a queue + level-size loop → shortest distance start→target
int bfs(List<List<Integer>> adj, int start, int target) {
    Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    boolean[] visited = new boolean[adj.size()];
    q.offer(start);
    visited[start] = true;          // mark the SOURCE at enqueue too
    int dist = 0;
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int sz = q.size();          // snapshot this level's width BEFORE the loop
        for (int i = 0; i < sz; i++) {
            int node = q.poll();
            if (node == target) return dist;
            for (int nei : adj.get(node)) {
                if (!visited[nei]) {
                    visited[nei] = true;   // mark BEFORE offering — the #1 bug
                    q.offer(nei);
                }
            }
        }
        dist++;                     // finished one level → distance grows by 1
    }
    return -1;                       // target unreachable
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Grid Graphs (Matrix as a Graph)
interview.deck: Stop seeing a matrix. See a graph whose nodes are cells and whose edges are the four cells next door — then DFS and BFS from Lessons 02 & 03 solve the entire island family unchanged.
interview.oneIdea: A grid int[][] g with R rows and C columns is a graph — you just never get handed an adjacency list. Each cell (r,c) is a node ; its edges are the in-bounds cells immediately around it: 4 (up/down/left/right) or, when diagonals count, 8. There is no buildAdj step because the neighbors are computed o...
interview.keyVisual:
static final int[][] DIRS = {{-1,0},{1,0},{0,-1},{0,1}}; // up, down, left, right

// flood one connected blob of '1's, marking visited IN PLACE
void dfs(char[][] g, int r, int c) {
    int R = g.length, C = g[0].length;
    if (r < 0 || r >= R || c < 0 || c >= C) return; // bounds guard FIRST — Java won't wrap
    if (g[r][c] != '1') return;                       // water or already-visited → stop
    g[r][c] = '0';                                    // MARK BEFORE recursing (sink the cell)
    for (int[] d : DIRS)
        dfs(g, r + d[0], c + d[1]);                   // recurse into all 4 neighbors
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Topological Sort
interview.deck: Line up the nodes of a directed acyclic graph so every dependency comes before the thing that needs it — and if you can't, you've just proven there's a cycle.
interview.oneIdea: A topological order is a linear arrangement of a directed graph's nodes such that for every edge u → v , u appears before v . Think "do prerequisites first." Such an order exists if and only if the graph is a DAG (directed, acyclic). The moment a cycle exists — A needs B, B needs C, C needs A — no n...
interview.keyVisual:
// Kahn's algorithm: produce a topological order, or detect a cycle.
int[] kahn(int n, int[][] edges) {       // edge {u, v} means u -> v (u before v)
    List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
    int[] indeg = new int[n];
    for (int[] e : edges) {
        adj.get(e[0]).add(e[1]);
        indeg[e[1]]++;                   // v gains one incoming edge
    }
    Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        if (indeg[i] == 0) q.offer(i);   // seed EVERY indegree-0 node (handles disconnected DAGs)
    int[] order = new int[n];
    int idx = 0;
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int u = q.poll();
        order[idx++] = u;                // u has no unmet prereqs → emit it
        for (int v : adj.get(u))
            if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.offer(v); // removing u frees v
    }
    return idx == n ? order : new int[0]; // idx < n → some nodes never reached 0 → CYCLE
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)
interview.deck: One parent[] array answers "are these two in the same group?" and "merge their groups" in near-constant time — the right tool the moment edges arrive one at a time .
interview.oneIdea: A Disjoint Set Union tracks a partition of n elements into groups. Each element points at a parent ; follow parents up to the root , which names the group. find(x) returns x's root; union(a, b) hangs one root under the other. Two optimizations make it fly: path compression (flatten the tree while yo...
interview.keyVisual:
class DSU {
    int[] parent, size;
    int count;                       // number of disjoint sets (components)

    DSU(int n) {
        parent = new int[n];
        size   = new int[n];
        count  = n;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { parent[i] = i; size[i] = 1; }  // each its own root
    }

    int find(int x) {                // iterative, with path compression
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];  // path halving: point x at its grandparent
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }

    boolean union(int a, int b) {    // union by size; false if already same set
        int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra == rb) return false;  // already joined → this edge would close a CYCLE
        if (size[ra] < size[rb]) { int t = ra; ra = rb; rb = t; }  // ra is the bigger tree
        parent[rb] = ra;             // smaller hangs under bigger
        size[ra] += size[rb];
        count--;                     // two sets became one
        return true;
    }
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Weighted Shortest Paths (Dijkstra & friends)
interview.deck: BFS only finds shortest paths when every edge costs 1. Add weights and you need a greedy min-heap (Dijkstra) — or a different tool when weights can be 0/1 or negative.
interview.oneIdea: On an unweighted graph, BFS works because every edge advances distance by exactly 1, so the frontier is naturally sorted by distance. The moment edges carry different costs, that guarantee breaks: the fewest- edges path is no longer the cheapest path. You now need an algorithm that always expands th...
interview.keyVisual:
// adjacency: adj.get(u) = list of {neighbor, weight}
int dijkstra(int n, List<List<int[]>> adj, int src, int dst) {
    int[] dist = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    dist[src] = 0;
    // min-heap ordered by distance-so-far (a[1]). WRONG direction = the classic bug.
    PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[1] - b[1]);
    pq.offer(new int[]{src, 0});       // {node, dist}
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        int[] top = pq.poll();
        int u = top[0], d = top[1];
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;     // LAZY DELETION — stale entry, already improved
        if (u == dst) return d;        // first pop of a node IS its final distance
        for (int[] e : adj.get(u)) {
            int v = e[0], w = e[1];
            if (dist[u] + w < dist[v]) {
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w; // relax
                pq.offer(new int[]{v, dist[v]}); // push the improved entry
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;                          // dst unreachable
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Minimum Spanning Tree (Kruskal & Prim)
interview.deck: Connect every node into one network for the least total cost. Two greedy builds — sort edges (Kruskal) or grow a tree (Prim) — and the same family of "minimum cost to connect" interview problems falls out.
interview.oneIdea: A spanning tree of a connected, undirected graph picks a subset of edges that touches all V nodes using exactly V − 1 edges and forms no cycle. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is the spanning tree whose edge weights sum to the smallest possible total. There are two greedy ways to build one, and both a...
interview.keyVisual:
// Returns total MST weight, or -1 if the graph is disconnected.
int kruskal(int n, int[][] edges) {       // edges[i] = {u, v, w}
    Arrays.sort(edges, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[2], b[2])); // cheapest first
    DSU dsu = new DSU(n);
    long total = 0;                        // long: summed weights can overflow int
    int used = 0;                          // edges added so far
    for (int[] e : edges) {
        if (dsu.union(e[0], e[1])) {       // union returns false if already same set
            total += e[2];
            if (++used == n - 1) break;    // V-1 edges → tree complete, stop early
        }
    }
    return used == n - 1 ? (int) total : -1; // fewer than V-1 → disconnected
}

interview.title: Advanced Graphs
interview.deck: The rarer-but-high-signal graph algorithms. Some you must own cold; most you only need to recognize and reach for the right name.
interview.oneIdea: The rarer-but-high-signal graph algorithms. Some you must own cold; most you only need to recognize and reach for the right name.
interview.keyVisual:
// LC 785: color[] holds 0 / 1, -1 = uncolored. BFS 2-coloring.
boolean isBipartite(int[][] graph) {
    int n = graph.length;
    int[] color = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(color, -1);
    for (int s = 0; s < n; s++) {        // graph may be DISCONNECTED — start everywhere
        if (color[s] != -1) continue;
        color[s] = 0;
        Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(s);
        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            int u = q.poll();
            for (int v : graph[u]) {
                if (color[v] == -1) {
                    color[v] = color[u] ^ 1;  // flip 0<->1
                    q.offer(v);
                } else if (color[v] == color[u]) {
                    return false;             // same color across an edge = odd cycle
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return true;
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Greedy Foundations
interview.deck: Take the best-looking option right now, never look back — a strategy that is usually wrong, occasionally provably perfect, and worth a fortune in OAs when you know which is which.
interview.oneIdea: A greedy algorithm builds a solution one step at a time, and at each step commits to the choice that looks best right now — no backtracking, no "what if". That makes it blazingly simple and fast (usually one sort plus one linear sweep), but also dangerous: a locally best choice can lock you out of t...
interview.keyVisual:
// LC 455 Assign Cookies: g[i] = child i's greed, s[j] = cookie j's size.
// Greedy: sort both; satisfy the easiest child with the smallest workable cookie.
int findContentChildren(int[] g, int[] s) {
    Arrays.sort(g);                      // 1. SORT by the safety dimension
    Arrays.sort(s);
    int child = 0;
    for (int cookie = 0; cookie < s.length && child < g.length; cookie++)
        if (s[cookie] >= g[child])       // 2. SWEEP: commit when the local choice works
            child++;                     // this child is done — never revisit
    return child;
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Scheduling & Intervals
interview.deck: One sorting decision — by end, not by start — turns "which meetings do I keep?" from a combinatorial nightmare into a single sweep. This is greedy's most famous provably-optimal win.
interview.oneIdea: When you must select as many non-overlapping intervals as possible, sort by end time and always keep the interval that finishes earliest . Why is that safe? Exchange argument: take any optimal schedule; its first meeting can be swapped for the earliest-finishing meeting overall, because finishing ea...
interview.keyVisual:
// LC 435 Non-overlapping Intervals: minimum removals so none overlap.
// Equivalent question: keep the MAXIMUM set of non-overlapping intervals.
int eraseOverlapIntervals(int[][] intervals) {
    Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[1], b[1])); // sort by END
    int kept = 0;
    int lastEnd = Integer.MIN_VALUE;     // finish time of the last kept interval
    for (int[] iv : intervals) {
        if (iv[0] >= lastEnd) {          // starts after last kept ends → compatible
            kept++;
            lastEnd = iv[1];             // COMMIT to the earliest-finishing choice
        }                                // else: overlaps → this one is a removal
    }
    return intervals.length - kept;      // removals = total − max kept
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Reachability & Heap Greedy
interview.deck: Two final greedy engines: a running frontier that answers "can I get there / how fast", and a heap that re-sorts the world after every choice. Plus the track cheat sheet.
interview.oneIdea: Some greedies don't sort at all. Reachability greedy sweeps once, maintaining the furthest index reachable so far — a frontier that only grows; a position is winnable iff the frontier never falls behind you (you saw this shape in Partition Labels). And when the "best next choice" changes after every...
interview.keyVisual:
// LC 55 Jump Game: nums[i] = max jump length from i. Can you reach the last index?
boolean canJump(int[] nums) {
    int reach = 0;                       // furthest index reachable so far
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        if (i > reach) return false;     // gap: frontier fell behind → stuck forever
        reach = Math.max(reach, i + nums[i]); // greedy: extend the frontier
        if (reach >= nums.length - 1) return true;
    }
    return true;                         // loop ended → last index was within reach
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Overlapping Intervals — Merge & Insert
interview.deck: Sort by start, sweep once, and every "do these ranges collide?" question collapses into a single comparison: cur.start <= prev.end .
interview.oneIdea: An interval [start, end] is a range on a number line. Unsorted, any pair might overlap and you're stuck with O(n²) pairwise checks. But sort by start and overlaps can only happen between neighbors in the sweep : as you walk left to right, the current interval either overlaps the last merged one ( cu...
interview.keyVisual:
int[][] merge(int[][] intervals) {
    Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])); // sort by START
    List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int[] cur : intervals) {
        if (!out.isEmpty() && cur[0] <= out.get(out.size() - 1)[1]) {
            // overlap: cur begins before (or exactly when) the last block ends
            int[] prev = out.get(out.size() - 1);
            prev[1] = Math.max(prev[1], cur[1]);   // max, NOT cur[1] — cur may be nested
        } else {
            out.add(cur);                          // gap → start a new block
        }
    }
    return out.toArray(new int[0][]);
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms

Track it either by reusing rooms (a min-heap of end times) or by sweeping time and counting +1 at every start and −1 at every end. (2) Maximum selection...
interview.keyVisual:
int minMeetingRooms(int[][] intervals) {
    Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])); // by START
    PriorityQueue<Integer> ends = new PriorityQueue<>();  // min-heap of end times = occupied rooms
    for (int[] m : intervals) {
        if (!ends.isEmpty() && ends.peek() <= m[0])
            ends.poll();               // earliest-freeing room is free by our start → reuse it
        ends.offer(m[1]);              // occupy a room (reused or brand new) until m[1]
    }
    return ends.size();                // rooms never shrink below the peak — heap size IS the answer
}

interview.oneIdea: A singly linked list is just nodes with one-way arrows. To reverse it in place , you walk the list once and flip each arrow to point backwards. The catch: the moment you flip cur.next , you lose your road forward. So you carry three pointers — prev (already-reversed part), cur (the node being flippe...
interview.keyVisual:
ListNode reverseList(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null;            // reversed part so far (starts empty)
    ListNode cur  = head;            // node whose arrow we're flipping now
    while (cur != null) {
        ListNode next = cur.next;    // 1. SAVE the road ahead before we cut it
        cur.next = prev;             // 2. FLIP the arrow backwards
        prev = cur;                  // 3. SLIDE prev up
        cur  = next;                 // 4. SLIDE cur up
    }
    return prev;                     // cur fell off the end; prev is the new head
}

Real interview problems wrap it: reverse every k nodes (count first, flip only full groups), rotate a list (no flipping at all — cut and re-tie a ring), or combine reversal with another pattern (find-mid + reverse + merge = Reorder List). The skill being tested is no...
interview.keyVisual:
ListNode reverseKGroup(ListNode head, int k) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);
    dummy.next = head;
    ListNode groupPrev = dummy;              // anchor: node just before the current group

    while (true) {
        ListNode kth = groupPrev;            // 1. PROBE: is there a full group of k?
        for (int i = 0; i < k && kth != null; i++) kth = kth.next;
        if (kth == null) break;              // fewer than k left → leave the tail as-is

        ListNode groupNext = kth.next;       // first node AFTER this group
        ListNode prev = groupNext;           // 2. FLIP: seed prev with groupNext…
        ListNode cur  = groupPrev.next;      //    …so the k-th flip auto-connects the back seam
        while (cur != groupNext) {           // standard Lesson-1 loop, k times
            ListNode next = cur.next;
            cur.next = prev;
            prev = cur;
            cur  = next;
        }
        ListNode newAnchor = groupPrev.next; // old group head = new group tail
        groupPrev.next = kth;                // 3. STITCH front seam: anchor → new head (kth)
        groupPrev = newAnchor;               // advance anchor to the group's tail
    }
    return dummy.next;
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: The Next-Greater Family
interview.deck: Every "for each element, find the nearest bigger/smaller one" question looks O(n²) — a stack that stays sorted answers all of them in one pass.
interview.oneIdea: Take Daily Temperatures: for each day, how many days until a warmer one? The naive answer scans right from every index — O(n²), and on a descending array it really does n²/2 work. Now flip the question: instead of each day searching forward for its answer, let each new day deliver answers backward ....
interview.keyVisual:
int[] dailyTemperatures(int[] t) {
    int n = t.length;
    int[] ans = new int[n];                // 0 = "no warmer day" (default)
    Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();// stack of INDICES; temps decreasing bottom→top
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        while (!st.isEmpty() && t[i] > t[st.peek()]) {
            int j = st.pop();              // day j just found its answer: it's day i
            ans[j] = i - j;                // distance — possible only because we stored indices
        }
        st.push(i);                        // i now waits for ITS next-greater
    }
    return ans;                            // whatever's left on the stack keeps ans = 0
}

interview.keyVisual:
int largestRectangleArea(int[] h) {
    int n = h.length, best = 0;
    Deque<Integer> st = new ArrayDeque<>();     // indices; heights increasing bottom→top
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {              // i == n is a virtual 0-height SENTINEL bar…
        int cur = (i == n) ? 0 : h[i];          // …that flushes every bar left on the stack
        while (!st.isEmpty() && cur < h[st.peek()]) {
            int mid = st.pop();                 // bar 'mid' now knows both walls:
            int height = h[mid];                //   right wall = i (first shorter on the right)
            int left = st.isEmpty() ? -1 : st.peek(); //   left wall = new top (first shorter on the left)
            int width = i - left - 1;           // strictly between the walls
            best = Math.max(best, height * width);
        }
        st.push(i);
    }
    return best;
}

class NumMatrix {
    private final int[][] S;                       // S[r][c] = sum of matrix[0..r-1][0..c-1]
    public NumMatrix(int[][] m) {
        int R = m.length, C = m[0].length;
        S = new int[R + 1][C + 1];                 // padded row 0 / col 0 stay zero — no edge cases
        for (int r = 1; r <= R; r++)
            for (int c = 1; c <= C; c++)
                S[r][c] = m[r-1][c-1] + S[r-1][c] + S[r][c-1] - S[r-1][c-1];
                // cell + above + left − overlap (counted twice)
    }
    public int sumRegion(int r1, int c1, int r2, int c2) {   // inclusive corners
        return S[r2+1][c2+1] - S[r1][c2+1] - S[r2+1][c1] + S[r1][c1];
        // whole − top strip − left strip + corner A added back
    }
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Fixed-Size Windows
interview.deck: Stop re-summing k elements from scratch — reuse the previous window's work by adding one element on the right and removing one on the left.
interview.oneIdea: Say you need the maximum sum of any subarray of length k . The naive move — the one you'd write from your 100-LeetCode instincts — is a double loop: for each start index i , sum nums[i..i+k-1] . That's O(n·k), and for n = 10⁵, k = 10⁴ it's dead on arrival. But look at two adjacent windows: [i..i+k-1...
interview.keyVisual:
// Maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of length k.
int maxSumFixed(int[] nums, int k) {
    long sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) sum += nums[i];   // phase 1: build first window [0..k-1]
    long best = sum;
    for (int r = k; r < nums.length; r++) {        // phase 2: slide right edge to r
        sum += nums[r];                            // add the entering element
        sum -= nums[r - k];                        // remove the leaving element (left edge)
        best = Math.max(best, sum);                // window is now [r-k+1 .. r]
    }
    return (int) best;
}

The window insight: define an invariant ("no character appears twice") and notice it's monotone — if a window violates it, every wider window containing it violates it too....
interview.keyVisual:
// Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (LC 3).
int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
    int[] count = new int[128];              // window state: freq of each ASCII char
    int l = 0, best = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < s.length(); r++) {
        count[s.charAt(r)]++;                // EXPAND: bring s[r] into the window
        while (count[s.charAt(r)] > 1) {     // SHRINK while invariant broken (a repeat exists)
            count[s.charAt(l)]--;            // evict s[l] and advance left edge
            l++;
        }
        best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);    // RECORD: window [l..r] is valid here
    }
    return best;
}

"How many subarrays have at most K distinct?" has a lovely closed form: after each expand-and-shrink, the window [l..r] is the largest valid window ending at r — so every suffix of it ( [l..r], [l+1..r], …, [r..r] ) is also valid (sh...
interview.keyVisual:
// Subarrays with K Different Integers (LC 992):
// exactly-K is not monotone → count it as atMost(K) − atMost(K−1).
int subarraysWithKDistinct(int[] nums, int k) {
    return atMost(nums, k) - atMost(nums, k - 1);
}

// #subarrays with AT MOST k distinct values — Lesson 2's shrink loop + one counting line.
int atMost(int[] nums, int k) {
    int[] count = new int[nums.length + 1];  // values are 1..n per constraints
    int distinct = 0, l = 0, total = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < nums.length; r++) {
        if (count[nums[r]]++ == 0) distinct++;
        while (distinct > k) {               // same shrink as LC 340
            if (--count[nums[l]] == 0) distinct--;
            l++;
        }
        total += r - l + 1;                  // every valid window ENDING at r: [l..r],[l+1..r],…,[r..r]
    }
    return total;
}

interview.keyVisual:
public class MergeSort {
    public static void sort(int[] arr, int left, int right) {
        if (left >= right) return;
        int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;
        sort(arr, left, mid);
        sort(arr, mid + 1, right);
        merge(arr, left, mid, right);
    }

    private static void merge(int[] arr, int left, int mid, int right) {
        int[] temp = new int[right - left + 1];
        int i = left, j = mid + 1, k = 0;

        while (i <= mid && j <= right) {
            if (arr[i] <= arr[j]) temp[k++] = arr[i++];
            else temp[k++] = arr[j++];
        }
        while (i <= mid) temp[k++] = arr[i++];
        while (j <= right) temp[k++] = arr[j++];

        System.arraycopy(temp, 0, arr, left, temp.length);
    }
}

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class MinStack {
    private final Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Deque<Integer> minStack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public void push(int val) {
        stack.push(val);
        if (minStack.isEmpty() || val <= minStack.peek()) {
            minStack.push(val);
        }
    }

    public void pop() {
        if (stack.pop().equals(minStack.peek())) {
            minStack.pop();
        }
    }

    public int top() { return stack.peek(); }
    public int getMin() { return minStack.peek(); }
}

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class MyQueue {
    private final Deque<Integer> inStack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final Deque<Integer> outStack = new ArrayDeque<>();

    public void push(int x) { inStack.push(x); }

    public int pop() {
        shiftStacks();
        return outStack.pop();
    }

    public int peek() {
        shiftStacks();
        return outStack.peek();
    }

    private void shiftStacks() {
        if (outStack.isEmpty()) {
            while (!inStack.isEmpty()) {
                outStack.push(inStack.pop()); // Inverts LIFO to FIFO!
            }
        }
    }
}

int findKthLargest(int[] nums, int k) {
    PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(); // MIN-heap: eviction door for the k largest
    for (int x : nums) {
        heap.offer(x);
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();  // evict the weakest of the current k
    }
    return heap.peek();                    // smallest survivor = kth largest
}

A MAX-heap holds the lower half (its top = biggest small number) and a MIN-heap holds the upper half (its top = smallest big number). The median lives at the seam between the two tops — O(1) to read — provided you rebalance so the sizes ...
interview.keyVisual:
class MedianFinder {
    private final PriorityQueue<Integer> lo =            // MAX-heap: lower half, top = its largest
        new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());
    private final PriorityQueue<Integer> hi =            // MIN-heap: upper half, top = its smallest
        new PriorityQueue<>();

    public void addNum(int num) {
        lo.offer(num);                // 1. drop into the lower half…
        hi.offer(lo.poll());          // 2. …but pass lo's max across — now every lo ≤ every hi
        if (hi.size() > lo.size())
            lo.offer(hi.poll());      // 3. rebalance: lo may equal or exceed hi by exactly 1
    }
    public double findMedian() {
        return lo.size() > hi.size()
            ? lo.peek()                          // odd count → lo's top IS the median
            : (lo.peek() + hi.peek()) / 2.0;     // even → average of the two seam values
    }
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: Iterative Traversals & Level Order
interview.deck: Recursion's call stack is just a stack — so build it yourself. Then swap the stack for a queue and the traversal flips from depth-first to level-by-level.
interview.oneIdea: Recursive traversal works because the call stack remembers every node you must come back to. Replace it with an explicit Deque<TreeNode> and you get the same traversal with no recursion — immune to stack overflow, pausable mid-stream (crucial for Kth Smallest, Lesson 5). And here's the deeper ...
interview.keyVisual:
// Iterative in-order. Time O(n), Space O(h) for the stack.
List<Integer> inorderTraversal(TreeNode root) {
    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null || !stack.isEmpty()) {
        while (cur != null) {          // slide down the LEFT spine…
            stack.push(cur);           // …remembering every node passed
            cur = cur.left;
        }
        cur = stack.pop();             // leftmost unvisited node
        out.add(cur.val);              // VISIT — this is the in-order moment
        cur = cur.right;               // now do its right subtree the same way
    }
    return out;
}

// The compute-from-children skeleton. Time O(n) — each node does O(1) work
// on top of its children's answers. Space O(h) recursion stack.
ReturnType solve(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return BASE;          // 1. what is the answer for an empty tree?
    ReturnType left  = solve(node.left);    // 2. trust recursion for the left subtree
    ReturnType right = solve(node.right);   // 3. …and the right subtree
    return combine(left, right, node);      // 4. O(1) merge — the only creative step
}

interview.subject: Data Structures & Algorithms
interview.title: LCA & Path Problems
interview.deck: Two of the most-asked medium/hard tree questions share one engine: a post-order pass where each node reports something useful upward while the real answer is assembled on the side.
interview.oneIdea: Both problems in this lesson are about paths that bend . The lowest common ancestor of p and q is the node where the path between them bends from "going up" to "going down". The maximum path sum is achieved at some node where two downward arms join. In both cases a single recursion answers a simpler...
interview.keyVisual:
// Returns: p or q if found in this subtree, the LCA if both were found
// below here, or null if this subtree contains neither.
// Time O(n), Space O(h).
TreeNode lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    if (root == null || root == p || root == q)
        return root;                       // found a target (or ran out) → report it up
    TreeNode left  = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left,  p, q);
    TreeNode right = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q);
    if (left != null && right != null)
        return root;                       // p and q split here → I am the bend → LCA
    return left != null ? left : right;    // pass up whichever side found something
}

interview.title: Binary Search Trees
interview.deck: One extra invariant — left < node < right, everywhere — turns a tree into a sorted structure with O(h) search, insert, and delete. Every BST problem is about exploiting or preserving that invariant.
interview.oneIdea: A BST's property is global, not local : every node in the left subtree — not just the left child — is smaller than the node, and every node in the right subtree is larger. That global ordering buys you three superpowers: (1) search is a walk — compare and go one way, O(h); (2) in-order traversal is ...
interview.keyVisual:
// Each node must lie strictly inside (lo, hi). Time O(n), Space O(h).
boolean isValidBST(TreeNode root) {
    return valid(root, null, null);        // null = unbounded (avoids MIN/MAX_VALUE traps)
}
boolean valid(TreeNode n, Integer lo, Integer hi) {
    if (n == null) return true;
    if (lo != null && n.val <= lo) return false;  // must be > every ancestor we went right from
    if (hi != null && n.val >= hi) return false;  // must be < every ancestor we went left from
    return valid(n.left,  lo, n.val)       // going left: my value caps the window above
        && valid(n.right, n.val, hi);      // going right: my value floors it below
}

interview.oneIdea: Every construction problem is the same two questions asked recursively: which element is the root? and which elements belong to its left subtree vs its right? Preorder (and postorder) answer the first — the root is the first (resp. last ) element. Inorder answers the second — everything left of the ...
interview.keyVisual:
// Time O(n) — each node built once, O(1) map lookup. Space O(n) map + O(h) stack.
Map<Integer, Integer> idx = new HashMap<>();  // value → its inorder position
int pre = 0;                                   // next unused preorder element

TreeNode buildTree(int[] preorder, int[] inorder) {
    for (int i = 0; i < inorder.length; i++) idx.put(inorder[i], i);
    return build(preorder, 0, inorder.length - 1);
}
TreeNode build(int[] preorder, int inLo, int inHi) {
    if (inLo > inHi) return null;              // this inorder range is empty → no subtree
    int rootVal = preorder[pre++];             // preorder ALWAYS knows the next root
    TreeNode root = new TreeNode(rootVal);
    int mid = idx.get(rootVal);                // inorder splits: [inLo..mid-1] | [mid+1..inHi]
    root.left  = build(preorder, inLo, mid - 1);  // MUST build left first — preorder order
    root.right = build(preorder, mid + 1, inHi);
    return root;
}

interview.title: Opposite-Ends Two Pointers
interview.deck: Start one pointer at each end, move them toward each other under a rule, and a brute-force O(n²) pair scan collapses into a single O(n) pass.
interview.oneIdea: You already know the naive way to find a pair in an array: two nested loops, try every (i, j) , O(n²). The two-pointer insight is that when the data has structure — it's sorted, or it's symmetric like a palindrome — you don't need to try every pair. Put left at index 0 and right at the last index. A...
interview.keyVisual:
// LC 167: sorted 1-indexed array, exactly one solution guaranteed.
int[] twoSum(int[] a, int target) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;         // one pointer per end
    while (l < r) {                      // strictly <: a pair needs two DIFFERENT indices
        int sum = a[l] + a[r];
        if (sum == target) return new int[]{l + 1, r + 1}; // problem wants 1-indexed
        if (sum < target) l++;           // sum too small → a[l] is exhausted: even a[r] couldn't save it
        else r--;                        // sum too big → a[r] is exhausted: even a[l] couldn't save it
    }
    return new int[]{-1, -1};            // unreachable here (solution guaranteed)
}

The fix: stop shifting and start rewriting . Run a fast pointer read over every element, and keep a slow pointer write marking the end of the "...
interview.keyVisual:
// LC 26: reader/writer compaction. Everything in [0, write) is deduped and final.
int removeDuplicates(int[] a) {
    int write = 1;                       // a[0] is always kept; first free slot is 1
    for (int read = 1; read < a.length; read++) {
        if (a[read] != a[write - 1]) {   // differs from the LAST KEPT value → keeper
            a[write] = a[read];          // write it into the good prefix
            write++;
        }                                // duplicate → read moves on, write stays
    }
    return write;                        // length of the deduped prefix; a[write..] is garbage
}

Every k-sum problem reduces to that: sort once, fix the first k−2 numbers with nested loops, and solve the last two with the two-pointer template . 3Sum = one outer loop + 2Sum inside → O(n²). 4Sum = two outer loops + 2S...
interview.keyVisual:
// LC 15: sort + anchor + two pointers. O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space (ignoring output).
List<List<Integer>> threeSum(int[] a) {
    Arrays.sort(a);                          // O(n log n), dwarfed by the O(n^2) scan
    List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 2; i++) {
        if (a[i] > 0) break;                 // smallest element positive → no zero-sum possible; done
        if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue; // DEDUP anchor: same anchor value → same triplets
        int l = i + 1, r = a.length - 1;     // 2Sum on the suffix, target -a[i]
        while (l < r) {
            int sum = a[i] + a[l] + a[r];
            if (sum < 0) l++;                // Lesson-1 elimination: a[l] is dead
            else if (sum > 0) r--;
            else {
                res.add(List.of(a[i], a[l], a[r]));
                l++; r--;                    // keep searching — more pairs may hit the target
                while (l < r && a[l] == a[l - 1]) l++; // DEDUP inner: hop over repeated values
                while (l < r && a[r] == a[r + 1]) r--;
            }
        }
    }
    return res;
}
