function debounce(fn, delay) {
  let timerId;                          // lives in the CLOSURE — survives between calls
  return function (...args) {          // regular function: preserves caller's `this`
    clearTimeout(timerId);              // a new call CANCELS the pending one
    timerId = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), delay);
  };                                    // arrow inside → inherits this + args correctly
}

const search = debounce((q) => console.log("API call:", q), 400);
search("h"); search("he"); search("hel");   // only "hel" fires, 400 ms after the last call

function throttle(fn, interval) {
  let last = 0;                         // timestamp of the last allowed run
  return function (...args) {
    const now = Date.now();
    if (now - last >= interval) {       // enough time passed? run and stamp
      last = now;
      fn.apply(this, args);
    }                                   // otherwise: silently drop this call
  };
}

window.addEventListener("scroll", throttle(() => console.log("tick"), 200));

Metric What It Measures Target Goal How to Optimize
LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) How long until the main hero image or primary text block finishes rendering on screen. < 2.5 seconds Use WebP/AVIF modern images, set priority on hero image, CDN caching, SSR/Edge rendering.
INP (Interaction to Next Paint) How quickly the page visually responds when a user clicks a button or taps an input. < 200 ms Break up long JavaScript tasks using requestIdleCallback() or web workers; avoid heavy sync loops on main thread.

import numpy as np

class NeuralNetworkFromScratch:
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim, output_dim, lr=0.1):
        self.lr = lr
        # He initialization for ReLU activation
        self.W1 = np.random.randn(input_dim, hidden_dim) * np.sqrt(2.0 / input_dim)
        self.b1 = np.zeros((1, hidden_dim))
        self.W2 = np.random.randn(hidden_dim, output_dim) * np.sqrt(2.0 / hidden_dim)
        self.b2 = np.zeros((1, output_dim))

    def _relu(self, z):
        return np.maximum(0, z)

    def _relu_deriv(self, z):
        return (z > 0).astype(float)

    def _softmax(self, z):
        shift = z - np.max(z, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
        exps = np.exp(shift)
        return exps / np.sum(exps, axis=-1, keepdims=True)

    def forward(self, X):
        self.X = X
        self.z1 = np.dot(X, self.W1) + self.b1
        self.a1 = self._relu(self.z1)
        self.z2 = np.dot(self.a1, self.W2) + self.b2
        self.a2 = self._softmax(self.z2)
        return self.a2

    def backward(self, y_true):
        N = self.X.shape[0]
        # 1. Output error (Softmax + Cross-Entropy derivative simplifies to: a2 - y_true)
        dz2 = (self.a2 - y_true) / N
        dW2 = np.dot(self.a1.T, dz2)
        db2 = np.sum(dz2, axis=0, keepdims=True)

        # 2. Backpropagate error into hidden layer
        da1 = np.dot(dz2, self.W2.T)
        dz1 = da1 * self._relu_deriv(self.z1)
        dW1 = np.dot(self.X.T, dz1)
        db1 = np.sum(dz1, axis=0, keepdims=True)

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

class SentimentLSTM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, embed_dim, hidden_dim, output_dim, n_layers=2):
        super(SentimentLSTM, self).__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim, padding_idx=0)
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(embed_dim, hidden_dim, num_layers=n_layers, 
                            batch_first=True, dropout=0.2, bidirectional=True)
        # Bidirectional outputs 2 * hidden_dim
        self.fc = nn.Linear(hidden_dim * 2, output_dim)

    def forward(self, text_tokens):
        # text_tokens shape: (batch_size, seq_len)
        embedded = self.embedding(text_tokens)
        
        # out: (batch, seq_len, 2*hidden_dim), (hidden, cell)
        lstm_out, (hidden, cell) = self.lstm(embedded)
        
        # Concatenate forward and backward final hidden states
        final_hidden = torch.cat((hidden[-2,:,:], hidden[-1,:,:]), dim=1)
        return self.fc(final_hidden)

ECB (Electronic Codebook) Each 16-byte block encrypted independently with the same key. FATALLY INSECURE. Identical plaintext blocks produce identical ciphertext blocks! (The famous Linux Tux penguin image remains clearly visible even after ECB encryption).

Metasploit decouples the Exploit (the mechanism used to take advantage of a so...
interview.keyVisual:
Payload FormatNaming ConventionMechanics & Trade-offs
Staged Payload windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp (separated by slashes) Injects a tiny Stager (few hundred bytes) into target memory, which opens a socket back to the attacker and downloads the full 1MB+ Stage. Essential when memory buffer space is limited.
Inline / Single windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_tcp (separated by underscore) Entire payload bundled into one contiguous blob. More stable in unreliable networks, but larger memory footprint.
Reverse Shell Target initiates connection OUT to Attacker (LHOST/LPORT) Industry Preferred. Evades perimeter inbound firewall blocks since outbound traffic (ports 80/443) is almost always permitted.
Bind Shell Target opens a listening port and waits for Attacker to connect Frequently blocked by target router firewalls and NAT.

The attacker cannot modify system files, access other users' data, or install...
interview.keyVisual:
VectorMisconfiguration / VulnerabilityExploitation Mechanism
Unquoted Service Paths Service path has spaces and is unquoted: C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe. Windows checks: C:\Program.exe, then C:\Program Files\My.exe. If attacker has write permissions in C:\, dropping Program.exe executes with SYSTEM privileges on reboot!
Token Impersonation (Potato Attacks) Service account possesses SeImpersonatePrivilege or SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege. Tools like JuicyPotato and PrintSpoofer trick a SYSTEM process (via RPC/Named Pipes) into authenticating locally and hijack its SYSTEM security token.
AlwaysInstallElevated Registry keys AlwaysInstallElevated = 1 in both HKLM and HKCU. Permits regular users to run .msi installers with elevated SYSTEM permissions. Attacker generates malicious MSI via msfvenom.

Crucial Exam Distinction

In Indian philosophy, Āstika does NOT mean "theist" (believer in God), and Nāstika does NOT mean "atheist"!

  • Āstika (Orthodox): Schools that accept the epistemic authority of the Vedas (even if they do not require a creator God, e.g. early Sāṃkhya and Mīmāṃsā).
  • Nāstika (Heterodox): Schools that do NOT accept the authority of the Vedas (Cārvāka, Buddhism, Jainism).

Key Characteristics of Takṣaśilā
  • Admission Age & Criteria: Minimum admission age was 16 years. Highly competitive; only mature, self-disciplined students were admitted.
  • Curriculum: 18 specialized arts and sciences (*Śilpas*), including Advanced Surgery, Medicine, Metallurgy, Military Archery, Warfare Tactics, Astronomy, Astrology, Commerce, and Pāṇinian Linguistics.
  • Illustrious Alumni:
    • Cāṇakya (Kauṭīlya): Master statesman and author of the Arthaśāstra taught here.
    • Candragupta Maurya: Founder of the Mauryan Empire received his military and governance training here under Chanakya.
    • Pāṇini: The greatest grammarian of human history studied and taught here.
    • Jīvaka: Personal physician to Buddha and King Bimbisāra studied medicine here for 7 years.
    • Caraka: The legendary father of Indian medicine completed his studies here.
  • Decline: Sacked and destroyed during the devastating invasions of the White Huns (Hephthalites) in the late 5th century CE.

sem.keyVisual:
Viṣṇu Śarmā's Pañcatantra (c. 300 BCE – 300 CE)

Composed to educate three indolent royal princes in political wisdom (*Nītiśāstra*) and practical worldly intelligence within six months using interconnected animal fables. Divided into 5 strategic books:

  1. Mitrabheda: The loss or estrangement of friends (dividing allies).
  2. Mitralābha: The winning of friends (the power of alliances).
  3. Kākolūkīyam: War and peace (the eternal conflict between crows and owls).
  4. Labdhapraṇāśam: Loss of gains (losing what you have earned through carelessness).
  5. Aparīkṣitakārakam: Ill-considered action (the danger of acting without investigation).

Global Impact: Translated into Pahlavi (Persian), Arabic (Kalīla wa-Dimna), Syriac, Greek, Latin, and over 50 European languages, becoming the most widely translated non-religious book in world history.

sem.oneIdea: Atomic theory in the Vaiśeṣika Sūtras, mind mastery in the Yoga Sūtras, and Advaita Vedānta philosophy.
sem.keyVisual:
Principles of Kaṇāda's Paramāṇu Theory
  • Indivisibility: If you divide matter infinitely without a stopping point, you encounter a logical fallacy (*Anavasthā Doṣa*). Therefore, matter must terminate in indivisible, infinitesimal, eternal particles called Paramāṇu (atoms).
  • Molecular Aggregation:
    • Two atoms combine to form a binary molecule: Dvyaṇuka (diatomic).
    • Three binary molecules combine to form a triad: Tryaṇuka or Trasa-reṇu (the smallest visible particle of matter, equivalent to a dust mote floating in a shaft of sunlight).
  • Four Elemental Atom Types: Pṛthvī (Earth atoms - possess smell), Jala (Water atoms - taste), Tejas (Fire/Light atoms - sight/color), Vāyu (Air atoms - touch). Ākāśa (Ether) is continuous, infinite, and non-atomic.
  • Chemical Transformation (*Pāka*): Heat induces chemical changes by breaking molecular bonds. Kaṇāda explained Pīlupāka (atomic heat absorption) vs Piṭharapāka (transformation of the compound as a whole, e.g. baking raw clay pots into red earthenware).

sem.oneIdea: Internal medicine in the Caraka Saṃhitā, plastic surgery and instruments in the Suśruta Saṃhitā, and neurosurgery by Jīvaka.
sem.keyVisual:
Core Diagnostic & Physiological Principles
  • Tridoṣa Theory: Human health represents dynamic equilibrium among three biological humors:
    • Vāta (Ether + Air): Governs all movement, respiration, nerve impulses, and circulation.
    • Pitta (Fire + Water): Governs metabolic transformation, digestion, body temperature, and intellect.
    • Kapha (Water + Earth): Governs structural stability, lubrication, cohesion, and tissue immunity.
    Disease (*Roga*) is defined as an imbalance (*Doṣa-vaiṣamya*); health (*Svāsthya*) is equilibrium.
  • Saptadhātu (Seven Body Tissues): The metabolic cascade where food converts sequentially into: Rasa (plasma) → Rakta (blood) → Māṃsa (muscle) → Meda (fat) → Asthi (bone) → Majjā (bone marrow) → Śukra (reproductive fluid) → yielding the supreme immune essence, Ojas.
  • Medical Ethics (Śiṣyopanayana): In the *Vimānasthāna*, Caraka outlines an ethical oath that every physician must take before practicing: to dedicate themselves selflessly to the cure of patients, never abandon the sick, treat poor patients free of charge, and strictly maintain medical confidentiality.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Overview of Operating Systems
sem.deck: What an operating system actually is, the two definitions worth quoting, the four-layer view of a computer system, the functions and components, and the interrupt-driven, dual-mode way an OS operates.
sem.oneIdea: What an operating system actually is, the two definitions worth quoting, the four-layer view of a computer system, the functions and components, and the interrupt-driven, dual-mode way an OS operates.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

This lesson is pure definition-and-list marks — the cheapest marks in the paper. Three shapes recur: “Define operating system and explain its functions” (5–10 marks), “Explain dual-mode operation and why it is needed”, and “Differentiate multiprogramming and multitasking”. Learn the two definitions verbatim, learn the function list as eight headings, and always draw the four-layer diagram — examiners give marks for the diagram alone.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Structures and Types of Operating Systems
sem.deck: The six ways an OS can be built — simple, monolithic, layered, microkernel, modular, hybrid — plus virtual machines, the eight types of operating system, and the system boot sequence.
sem.oneIdea: The six ways an OS can be built — simple, monolithic, layered, microkernel, modular, hybrid — plus virtual machines, the eight types of operating system, and the system boot sequence.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two guaranteed questions live here. “Explain the structures of an operating system with diagrams” is a 10-mark answer — you need a labelled diagram for each, and the microkernel one especially. “Explain the types of operating system” is 5–10 marks and is marked on breadth: name all eight, one line and one example each. Monolithic vs microkernel is the single most-asked comparison in this unit — memorise that table.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Operating System Services, User Interfaces and System Programs
sem.deck: The eight services split into two groups, the three kinds of user interface, the six categories of system program, and the debugging facilities the OS provides.
sem.oneIdea: The eight services split into two groups, the three kinds of user interface, the six categories of system program, and the debugging facilities the OS provides.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

A reliable 5-mark question: “List and explain the services provided by an operating system.” The mark is won by splitting them into two groups — services that help the user, and services that ensure efficient system operation — before listing. Most students just list eight things; the split is what looks like an answer rather than a recall. CLI vs GUI is a short-note favourite, and system program vs application program is a one-liner that appears in objective sections.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: System Calls
sem.deck: What a system call is, how it differs from an API, the three ways parameters are passed, the six categories with their UNIX and Windows names, and the standard cp trace that examiners love.
sem.oneIdea: What a system call is, how it differs from an API, the three ways parameters are passed, the six categories with their UNIX and Windows names, and the standard cp trace that examiners love.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three question shapes. “What is a system call? Explain its types” — 10 marks, and the mark is on the six categories with two or three examples each; learn the UNIX/Windows table. “Explain the methods of passing parameters to the OS” — exactly three methods, always. “Describe the sequence of system calls to copy one file to another” — a stock question with a stock answer, given in full below. Also learn system call vs API vs function call, which appears in every objective section.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Process Concept, Scheduling and Operations
sem.deck: Process vs program, the five-state diagram, the Process Control Block, scheduling queues and the three schedulers, context switching, process creation and termination, and the fork() numericals.
sem.oneIdea: Process vs program, the five-state diagram, the Process Control Block, scheduling queues and the three schedulers, context switching, process creation and termination, and the fork() numericals.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

The process state diagram is the single most drawn diagram in this subject — five states, five labelled transitions, and every transition named. Draw it for any question that mentions processes at all. “What is a PCB? What does it contain?” is a guaranteed 5-marker; learn the eight fields. “Differentiate long-term, short-term and medium-term scheduler” is a guaranteed comparison table. And fork() output counting is an objective-question staple — 2n is the whole trick.

sem.oneIdea: Why processes cooperate, the two IPC models compared, the bounded-buffer producer–consumer code, direct and indirect message passing, blocking and non-blocking, buffering, and the four real IPC systems.

Exam strategy

“Explain the two models of interprocess communication with diagrams” is the 10-mark question here, and the comparison table below is the answer. The bounded-buffer producer–consumer code is worth writing out — it appears again in Unit II with semaphores, so learning it now pays twice. Also learn the three design questions of message passing (direct/indirect, synchronous/asynchronous, buffering), because “discuss the issues in message passing” is exactly those three.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Threads and Multithreading
sem.deck: Single-threaded and multithreaded processes, what a thread owns and what it shares, the four benefits, user and kernel threads, the three multithreading models, multicore programming, Amdahl's law, and the threading issues.
sem.oneIdea: Single-threaded and multithreaded processes, what a thread owns and what it shares, the four benefits, user and kernel threads, the three multithreading models, multicore programming, Amdahl's law, and the threading issues.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two certainties. “Differentiate process and thread” — a table, every year, and the winning line is what is shared versus what is private. “Explain the multithreading models with diagrams” — three models, three diagrams, one advantage and one disadvantage each. The four benefits (responsiveness, resource sharing, economy, scalability) are a 4-mark list you should be able to write without thinking. Amdahl's law is the only numerical here, and it is easy marks when it appears.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: CPU Scheduling — Concepts and Criteria
sem.deck: The CPU–I/O burst cycle, what the short-term scheduler and the dispatcher each do, preemptive versus non-preemptive scheduling, and the five criteria with the exact formulas every numerical depends on.
sem.oneIdea: The CPU–I/O burst cycle, what the short-term scheduler and the dispatcher each do, preemptive versus non-preemptive scheduling, and the five criteria with the exact formulas every numerical depends on.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Read this before Lesson 9 — every numerical in the paper depends on the four formulas below. The single most common mistake in this whole subject is confusing waiting time with turnaround time, or forgetting to subtract the arrival time. Learn the four definitions as equations, not as sentences. The preemptive vs non-preemptive table and the four situations in which scheduling decisions occur are both short-answer questions in their own right.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms — the Full Drill
sem.deck: FCFS, SJF, SRTF, priority in both forms and Round Robin at three quantum values — twelve problems, every Gantt chart drawn and every average computed, plus the convoy effect, starvation and ageing.
sem.oneIdea: FCFS, SJF, SRTF, priority in both forms and Round Robin at three quantum values — twelve problems, every Gantt chart drawn and every average computed, plus the convoy effect, starvation and ageing.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

This is the guaranteed question in the paper — 10 to 15 marks, every single year, and it is purely mechanical. Work every problem below with a pen before checking the answer; reading them does nothing. The examiner almost always gives a table of arrival and burst times and asks for two or three algorithms on the same data, then asks which is best. The comparison table at the end of this lesson answers that last part in one sentence.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Multilevel Queue, Feedback Queue and Multiple-Processor Scheduling
sem.deck: Multilevel queue scheduling with a worked trace, multilevel feedback queues with their five parameters and a full three-level trace, and multiple-processor scheduling — asymmetric and symmetric, affinity, load balancing and multicore.
sem.oneIdea: Multilevel queue scheduling with a worked trace, multilevel feedback queues with their five parameters and a full three-level trace, and multiple-processor scheduling — asymmetric and symmetric, affinity, load balancing and multicore.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two things are asked here. “Explain multilevel queue and multilevel feedback queue scheduling” — the mark hinges on one distinction: in a multilevel queue a process never changes queue; in a feedback queue it does. Say that sentence first. “Explain multiple-processor scheduling” is a theory answer: asymmetric vs symmetric, processor affinity, load balancing, and the two multicore terms. The MLFQ trace below is the harder numerical, and it does appear.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Process Synchronisation and the Critical-Section Problem
sem.deck: The race condition worked instruction by instruction, the structure of a critical section, the three conditions any solution must satisfy, the turn and flag attempts, Peterson's solution, the hardware instructions, and mutex locks.
sem.oneIdea: The race condition worked instruction by instruction, the structure of a critical section, the three conditions any solution must satisfy, the turn and flag attempts, Peterson's solution, the hardware instructions, and mutex locks.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“What is the critical-section problem? State the conditions any solution must satisfy” is a certainty — the three conditions are mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting, and you must be able to define each in one sentence. Peterson's solution is a full 10-mark answer: write the code, then prove all three conditions hold. The race-condition trace below is the standard way to open a synchronisation answer, and it is worth memorising as a five-line table.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Semaphores
sem.deck: The wait and signal operations, binary and counting semaphores, the block–wakeup implementation that removes busy waiting, enforcing execution order, and the three things that still go wrong — deadlock, starvation and priority inversion.
sem.oneIdea: The wait and signal operations, binary and counting semaphores, the block–wakeup implementation that removes busy waiting, enforcing execution order, and the three things that still go wrong — deadlock, starvation and priority inversion.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three certainties. “What is a semaphore? Explain wait and signal” — write both operations as code, and stress that they are atomic. “Differentiate binary and counting semaphore” — a table. Semaphore value numericals — count the P's and V's, and know that a negative value is the number of blocked processes; that single fact answers most objective questions on this topic. Priority inversion, with the Mars Pathfinder story, is a reliable short note.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Classic Problems of Synchronisation
sem.deck: The bounded buffer, readers–writers in both variants, dining philosophers with the deadlock and its four fixes, and the sleeping barber — every solution written in full with the semaphores named and initialised.
sem.oneIdea: The bounded buffer, readers–writers in both variants, dining philosophers with the deadlock and its four fixes, and the sleeping barber — every solution written in full with the semaphores named and initialised.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

These three problems are the highest-value theory in Unit II — one of them appears in every paper, usually for 10 marks. The answer format is fixed and you should follow it exactly: (1) state the problem, (2) list the shared variables with their initial values, (3) write the producer/consumer or reader/writer code, (4) explain why it works, (5) name the remaining flaw. For dining philosophers, the marks are in the deadlock scenario and its four remedies, not in the code. Always state the initial value of every semaphore — that line alone is often worth a mark.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Monitors
sem.deck: Why semaphores were not enough, the monitor construct and its automatic mutual exclusion, condition variables with wait and signal, the signal-and-wait versus signal-and-continue question, the dining-philosophers monitor, and implementing a monitor with semaphores.
sem.oneIdea: Why semaphores were not enough, the monitor construct and its automatic mutual exclusion, condition variables with wait and signal, the signal-and-wait versus signal-and-continue question, the dining-philosophers monitor, and implementing a monitor with semaphores.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“What is a monitor? How does it differ from a semaphore?” is the question, and it is worth 5–10 marks. The winning line is: a monitor provides mutual exclusion automatically, so the programmer cannot forget it; a semaphore relies entirely on the programmer. Draw the schematic view — shared data, procedures, entry queue — and know that x.signal() on a condition variable with nobody waiting has no effect, which is exactly where it differs from a semaphore's signal(). The dining-philosophers monitor is the standard long answer.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Deadlock Characterisation
sem.deck: The system model, the four necessary conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait), resource-allocation graphs, and how to tell from a RAG whether deadlock exists.
sem.oneIdea: The system model, the four necessary conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait), resource-allocation graphs, and how to tell from a RAG whether deadlock exists.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Name and explain the four necessary conditions for deadlock is a guaranteed 5-marker. Draw a resource-allocation graph and determine if deadlock exists is a 5–10 marker. These are definitional — learn them word-perfect.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Deadlock Prevention and Avoidance
sem.deck: Prevention by breaking one of the four conditions, avoidance using the safe-state concept, and the Banker’s Algorithm — the single most important numerical in this unit.
sem.oneIdea: Prevention by breaking one of the four conditions, avoidance using the safe-state concept, and the Banker’s Algorithm — the single most important numerical in this unit.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Banker’s Algorithm is a guaranteed 10–15 mark numerical. You must compute Need = Max − Allocation, then find a safe sequence. Show the Work vector at every step. Prevention is a 5-mark theory question.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Deadlock Detection and Recovery
sem.deck: The detection algorithm (wait-for graph for single-instance, Banker’s-style for multi-instance), when to run it, and the four recovery strategies.
sem.oneIdea: The detection algorithm (wait-for graph for single-instance, Banker’s-style for multi-instance), when to run it, and the four recovery strategies.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain deadlock detection algorithm” or “differentiate prevention, avoidance, and detection”. Recovery is a short-note — know process termination and resource preemption.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Memory Management — Contiguous Allocation, Paging and Segmentation
sem.deck: Objectives of memory management, overlays and swapping, contiguous allocation (fixed and variable partitions), first/best/worst fit, internal vs external fragmentation, paging with page tables, and segmentation.
sem.oneIdea: Objectives of memory management, overlays and swapping, contiguous allocation (fixed and variable partitions), first/best/worst fit, internal vs external fragmentation, paging with page tables, and segmentation.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Paging address translation (given logical address, page size, find page number and offset, then physical address) is a guaranteed numerical. Internal vs external fragmentation and first/best/worst fit are guaranteed short-notes.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Virtual Memory and Demand Paging
sem.deck: Why virtual memory exists, demand paging with lazy swapper, page fault handling, the effective access time formula, and copy-on-write.
sem.oneIdea: Why virtual memory exists, demand paging with lazy swapper, page fault handling, the effective access time formula, and copy-on-write.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain demand paging with page fault handling steps” is a guaranteed 5–10 marker. The effective access time numerical (given page fault rate and access times) is a common calculation.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Page Replacement, Frame Allocation and Thrashing
sem.deck: FIFO, Optimal, LRU page replacement algorithms with full worked traces, Belady’s anomaly, frame allocation policies, the working-set model, and thrashing.
sem.oneIdea: FIFO, Optimal, LRU page replacement algorithms with full worked traces, Belady’s anomaly, frame allocation policies, the working-set model, and thrashing.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Page replacement is a guaranteed 10–15 mark numerical. You will be given a reference string and frame count. Trace FIFO, Optimal and LRU, count page faults. Know Belady’s anomaly (FIFO can have MORE faults with MORE frames).

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: File System Interface
sem.deck: The concept of a file, file attributes and operations, access methods (sequential, direct, indexed), directory structure (single-level, two-level, tree, acyclic graph, general graph), mounting, and protection.
sem.oneIdea: The concept of a file, file attributes and operations, access methods (sequential, direct, indexed), directory structure (single-level, two-level, tree, acyclic graph, general graph), mounting, and protection.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain directory structures with diagrams” is a guaranteed 5–10 marker. “Compare sequential and direct access” is a standard short-note.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: File System Implementation and Allocation Methods
sem.deck: On-disk structures (boot block, super block, directory implementation), three allocation methods (contiguous, linked, indexed), and free-space management (bit vector, linked list).
sem.oneIdea: On-disk structures (boot block, super block, directory implementation), three allocation methods (contiguous, linked, indexed), and free-space management (bit vector, linked list).
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Compare contiguous, linked, and indexed allocation” is a guaranteed 10-marker. Draw diagrams for each. Free-space management with bit vectors is a common short-note.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Disk Scheduling and RAID
sem.deck: Disk structure (CHS), five scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK) with worked traces, swap-space management, and RAID levels.
sem.oneIdea: Disk structure (CHS), five scheduling algorithms (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK) with worked traces, swap-space management, and RAID levels.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Disk scheduling is a guaranteed 10-mark numerical. Given a queue of cylinder requests and the current head position, trace FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK and compute total head movement. RAID levels are a common short-note.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: I/O Hardware and Interfaces
sem.deck: I/O devices, device controllers, memory-mapped vs port-mapped I/O, polling (busy-waiting), interrupt-driven I/O, and Direct Memory Access (DMA) with cycle stealing.
sem.oneIdea: I/O devices, device controllers, memory-mapped vs port-mapped I/O, polling (busy-waiting), interrupt-driven I/O, and Direct Memory Access (DMA) with cycle stealing.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Compare Polling, Interrupts, and Direct Memory Access (DMA) for I/O operations” is a guaranteed 7-to-10 mark question. Always draw the DMA architecture diagram and contrast cycle stealing with burst mode.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Kernel I/O Subsystem
sem.deck: I/O scheduling, buffering mechanisms (single, double, circular), caching vs spooling, device reservation, error handling, and the STREAMS architecture.
sem.oneIdea: I/O scheduling, buffering mechanisms (single, double, circular), caching vs spooling, device reservation, error handling, and the STREAMS architecture.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain the services provided by the Kernel I/O Subsystem” and “Differentiate between Caching, Buffering, and Spooling” are recurrent 8-to-10 mark questions. Work through the timing arithmetic for single vs double buffering.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Protection and the Access Matrix
sem.deck: Goals and principles of OS protection, domains of protection, the Access Matrix model, implementing access matrices (ACLs vs Capability Lists), and revocation of access rights.
sem.oneIdea: Goals and principles of OS protection, domains of protection, the Access Matrix model, implementing access matrices (ACLs vs Capability Lists), and revocation of access rights.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain the Access Matrix model and compare Access Control Lists (ACL) with Capability Lists (C-Lists)” is a guaranteed 10-mark question. Provide an explicit tabular matrix diagram and contrast revocation difficulty in both implementations.

sem.subject: Operating Systems (Semester)
sem.title: Operating System Security and Threats
sem.deck: The security problem, program threats (Trojans, trapdoors, logic bombs, buffer overflows), system and network threats (DoS, port scanning), and Linux/Windows modern security case studies (SELinux and Windows UAC).
sem.oneIdea: The security problem, program threats (Trojans, trapdoors, logic bombs, buffer overflows), system and network threats (DoS, port scanning), and Linux/Windows modern security case studies (SELinux and Windows UAC).
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain program threats and system threats with examples” and “Compare Linux (SELinux) and Windows OS security architectures” are recurrent 7-to-10 mark questions. Define the standard threat taxonomy and detail Mandatory Access Control (MAC) vs Discretionary Access Control (DAC).

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: What a Computer Network Is
sem.deck: Definitions, the five components, the four characteristics of data communication, the three network criteria, and the performance numericals. The definitions here are the ones every later answer in this subject is built out of.
sem.oneIdea: Definitions, the five components, the four characteristics of data communication, the three network criteria, and the performance numericals. The definitions here are the ones every later answer in this subject is built out of.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three questions come out of this lesson. (1) "Define data communication and list its components" — 5 marks, pure recall, draw the five-box diagram. (2) "What are the criteria of a good network?" — 5 marks, three headings with sub-points. (3) A latency numerical — propagation + transmission delay. Learn the two formulas and you cannot lose those marks.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Data Flow and Connection Types
sem.deck: Simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex — a named syllabus topic and a guaranteed short question. Plus point-to-point vs multipoint connections, serial vs parallel transmission, and the unicast/broadcast/multicast trio.
sem.oneIdea: Simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex — a named syllabus topic and a guaranteed short question. Plus point-to-point vs multipoint connections, serial vs parallel transmission, and the unicast/broadcast/multicast trio.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Explain the three modes of data flow with diagrams" is a 5-mark question that takes three minutes if you have the arrow diagrams memorised. Always draw the arrows — three tiny sketches score more reliably than three paragraphs. The keyboard/monitor, walkie-talkie and telephone examples are the ones examiners expect; use those, not invented ones.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Types of Networks: PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN
sem.deck: Networks classified by geographic span, then by architecture. One comparison table carries most of the marks here — the rest is vocabulary you must not mix up: internet vs Internet, intranet vs extranet.
sem.oneIdea: Networks classified by geographic span, then by architecture. One comparison table carries most of the marks here — the rest is vocabulary you must not mix up: internet vs Internet, intranet vs extranet.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Differentiate between LAN, MAN and WAN" is close to guaranteed — a 5-mark table. Give it six or seven rows: span, ownership, speed, error rate, cost, technology, example. Add PAN as a fourth column only if the question names it. Then keep two spare lines for client-server vs peer-to-peer, which is asked separately just as often.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Network Topologies
sem.deck: Mesh, star, bus, ring, tree and hybrid — each with its link count, its advantages, its disadvantages, and the one formula that turns this descriptive topic into a numerical you can score on with certainty.
sem.oneIdea: Mesh, star, bus, ring, tree and hybrid — each with its link count, its advantages, its disadvantages, and the one formula that turns this descriptive topic into a numerical you can score on with certainty.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two questions live here. (1) "Explain any four network topologies with diagrams, advantages and disadvantages" — 10 marks, and the single most-asked question in Unit I. Draw every diagram; a topology answer without diagrams loses marks no matter how good the prose is. (2) The mesh link formula — n(n − 1)/2. Small, mechanical, and it appears as a 2-mark numerical constantly.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: The OSI Reference Model
sem.deck: Seven layers, their functions, their PDUs, their devices and their protocols — plus encapsulation. This is the largest single question in Unit I and the model every later unit is organised around.
sem.oneIdea: Seven layers, their functions, their PDUs, their devices and their protocols — plus encapsulation. This is the largest single question in Unit I and the model every later unit is organised around.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Explain the OSI reference model with a neat diagram" is a 10-mark question and near-certain. Structure it as: definition → why layering → the seven-layer diagram → two or three functions per layer → encapsulation. Do not write a paragraph per layer; write a heading plus bullets per layer. And draw the stack twice, sender and receiver, with the arrow going down one side and up the other — that diagram alone is worth two marks.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: The TCP/IP Model, and OSI vs TCP/IP
sem.deck: The model the Internet actually runs on, the protocols that sit in each of its layers, the mapping onto OSI, and the comparison table — which is the highest-probability question in the whole unit.
sem.oneIdea: The model the Internet actually runs on, the protocols that sit in each of its layers, the mapping onto OSI, and the comparison table — which is the highest-probability question in the whole unit.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Compare the OSI and TCP/IP reference models" is the single most likely question in Unit I. Answer it as a table of 8–10 rows, preceded by the side-by-side layer diagram, and followed by one short paragraph on why TCP/IP won. That structure — diagram, table, closing paragraph — is a full-mark answer and takes eight minutes.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Analog and Digital Data and Signals
sem.deck: The physical layer starts here: what data and signals are, the three attributes of a sine wave, the time and frequency domains, bandwidth, and the three transmission impairments. Mostly definitions and small numericals — cheap marks if you learn the vocabulary precisely.
sem.oneIdea: The physical layer starts here: what data and signals are, the three attributes of a sine wave, the time and frequency domains, bandwidth, and the three transmission impairments. Mostly definitions and small numericals — cheap marks if you learn the vocabulary precisely.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

This topic is asked in small pieces, not one big question: "differentiate analog and digital signals" (3 marks), "define bandwidth of a composite signal" (2 marks), "explain transmission impairments" (5 marks), plus a one-line dB or SNR calculation. Learn the definitions and units exactly — that is where the marks are, not in explanation.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Data Rate Limits and Performance Analysis
sem.deck: Nyquist and Shannon — two formulas, four worked numericals, and the one rule for deciding which to use. This is the most reliably scoring topic in Unit II because the answers are objectively right or wrong.
sem.oneIdea: Nyquist and Shannon — two formulas, four worked numericals, and the one rule for deciding which to use. This is the most reliably scoring topic in Unit II because the answers are objectively right or wrong.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

A Nyquist or Shannon numerical appears in essentially every paper. Learn both formulas, learn the one-line rule for which applies, and always finish with the combined-use conclusion: when both are given, the Shannon limit is the ceiling and the Nyquist formula tells you how many signal levels to use to reach it. That last step is where most students stop early and lose marks.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Line Coding
sem.deck: Converting bits into signals. Eight schemes, the four characteristics used to judge them, and the one skill the exam actually tests: drawing the waveform for a given bit stream without making an error.
sem.oneIdea: Converting bits into signals. Eight schemes, the four characteristics used to judge them, and the one skill the exam actually tests: drawing the waveform for a given bit stream without making an error.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

The question is almost always "encode the bit stream 10110010 using NRZ-L, NRZ-I, Manchester and Differential Manchester" — a drawing question worth 5–10 marks. Marks come from the waveform being right, not from prose. Draw a labelled time axis, mark the bit boundaries with dotted vertical lines, and state your convention (which level is 1) before you start. An unstated convention is the commonest reason a correct-looking answer loses marks.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Bandwidth Utilization: Multiplexing and Spread Spectrum
sem.deck: Two opposite ideas with one name. Multiplexing shares a wide link between many users to save bandwidth; spread spectrum deliberately wastes bandwidth to buy security. FDM, WDM, TDM, FHSS and DSSS — with the TDM numericals that carry the marks.
sem.oneIdea: Two opposite ideas with one name. Multiplexing shares a wide link between many users to save bandwidth; spread spectrum deliberately wastes bandwidth to buy security. FDM, WDM, TDM, FHSS and DSSS — with the TDM numericals that carry the marks.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two questions live here. (1) "Explain FDM and TDM with diagrams" — a 5-mark comparison; draw both, and be explicit that FDM divides frequency while TDM divides time. (2) A TDM numerical — frame size, frame rate, or bit duration. Learn the four TDM formulas; they are short and mechanical. Spread spectrum is usually a 3-mark "differentiate FHSS and DSSS".

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Transmission Media
sem.deck: Guided and unguided media — twisted pair, coaxial, fibre optic, radio, microwave and infrared. A descriptive topic with a fixed structure: definition, construction, advantages, disadvantages, applications. Learn the structure and every sub-question answers itself.
sem.oneIdea: Guided and unguided media — twisted pair, coaxial, fibre optic, radio, microwave and infrared. A descriptive topic with a fixed structure: definition, construction, advantages, disadvantages, applications. Learn the structure and every sub-question answers itself.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Asked as "Explain guided transmission media with diagrams" (10 marks) or "Compare twisted pair, coaxial and fibre optic" (5 marks, table). For the long version, use the same five headings for each medium — construction, how it carries the signal, advantages, disadvantages, applications — and draw the cross-section of each cable. Consistency of structure reads as command of the material and is quick to write.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Switching
sem.deck: Circuit switching, packet switching (datagram and virtual circuit) and message switching. One comparison table carries this topic, plus a delay numerical that shows exactly why packet switching won.
sem.oneIdea: Circuit switching, packet switching (datagram and virtual circuit) and message switching. One comparison table carries this topic, plus a delay numerical that shows exactly why packet switching won.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Compare circuit switching and packet switching" is a certainty — 5 to 10 marks, answered as a table of 8–10 rows. The sub-question that separates good answers from average ones is datagram vs virtual circuit, so keep three rows for it. Draw the three phases of circuit switching (setup, data transfer, teardown) as a timeline; it is quick and it is worth a mark.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Error Detection and Correction
sem.deck: The most numerical lesson in the subject. Parity, LRC, checksum, CRC and Hamming code — each worked end to end with the arithmetic shown. CRC and Hamming between them appear in almost every paper.
sem.oneIdea: The most numerical lesson in the subject. Parity, LRC, checksum, CRC and Hamming code — each worked end to end with the arithmetic shown. CRC and Hamming between them appear in almost every paper.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Expect a CRC numerical and a Hamming code numerical. Together they are often 15–20 marks, and they are objectively markable — you either get them right or you do not. Do the division and the parity checks slowly; almost every lost mark here is arithmetic, not understanding. Always verify your own answer at the receiver end: divide the codeword again and show the remainder is zero. That verification is usually worth a mark and it catches your own mistakes.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Framing, Flow and Error Control
sem.deck: Byte stuffing and bit stuffing, then the three sliding-window protocols — Stop-and-Wait ARQ, Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat — with the efficiency formulas and the window-size rules that the numericals are built from.
sem.oneIdea: Byte stuffing and bit stuffing, then the three sliding-window protocols — Stop-and-Wait ARQ, Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat — with the efficiency formulas and the window-size rules that the numericals are built from.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three questions come from here. (1) Bit stuffing — a 3-mark "apply bit stuffing to this bit stream", pure mechanics. (2) Compare the three ARQ protocols — a table, 5–10 marks; keep a row for window sizes, it is the most-asked single fact. (3) An efficiency numerical — compute a, then apply the formula. Learn a = Tp/Tt first; every efficiency formula in this lesson is built on it.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: HDLC and Point-to-Point Protocol
sem.deck: Two named data link protocols. HDLC gives you configurations, transfer modes and three frame types; PPP gives you a frame format, four transition phases and two authentication protocols. Both are descriptive — diagram-and-list questions, no numericals.
sem.oneIdea: Two named data link protocols. HDLC gives you configurations, transfer modes and three frame types; PPP gives you a frame format, four transition phases and two authentication protocols. Both are descriptive — diagram-and-list questions, no numericals.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Asked as "Explain HDLC with its frame format" and "Explain PPP and its frame format" — 5 marks each, sometimes combined into 10. Draw the frame format as a labelled box diagram with byte counts; that diagram is most of the mark. Then list the field meanings in one line each. For HDLC, the three frame types (I, S, U) are the part most often asked on its own.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Multiple Access: Random Access
sem.deck: ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA. Two throughput formulas, the three persistence methods, the minimum-frame-size rule, and the reason wireless cannot use the same mechanism as wired Ethernet.
sem.oneIdea: ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD and CSMA/CA. Two throughput formulas, the three persistence methods, the minimum-frame-size rule, and the reason wireless cannot use the same mechanism as wired Ethernet.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three near-certain questions. (1) Pure vs slotted ALOHA with the throughput formulas and their maxima — memorise 0.184 at G = 0.5 and 0.368 at G = 1; those two numbers alone often carry the question. (2) The three persistence methods, with a flowchart for each. (3) CSMA/CD vs CSMA/CA, and why wireless needs avoidance rather than detection — that "why" is where the marks separate.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Controlled Access and Channelization
sem.deck: The two collision-free families. Reservation, polling and token passing decide who may speak ; FDMA, TDMA and CDMA divide the channel itself . Includes a fully worked CDMA encode-and-decode — the one numerical in this lesson.
sem.oneIdea: The two collision-free families. Reservation, polling and token passing decide who may speak ; FDMA, TDMA and CDMA divide the channel itself . Includes a fully worked CDMA encode-and-decode — the one numerical in this lesson.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two questions. (1) "Explain controlled access methods" — 5 marks, three short paragraphs with a diagram each; the token-passing half is the part most often asked alone. (2) "Differentiate FDMA, TDMA and CDMA" — a three-column table, and if CDMA appears as a numerical, the chip-code walkthrough below is exactly the shape it takes. Do not confuse FDMA/TDMA (access methods, many stations) with FDM/TDM (multiplexing techniques, one sender's streams) — examiners set that trap deliberately.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Ethernet
sem.deck: The IEEE 802 model, the Ethernet frame format field by field, MAC addressing, the minimum and maximum frame sizes and where they come from, and the four generations from 10 Mbps to 10 Gbps. The last lesson of Unit II.
sem.oneIdea: The IEEE 802 model, the Ethernet frame format field by field, MAC addressing, the minimum and maximum frame sizes and where they come from, and the four generations from 10 Mbps to 10 Gbps. The last lesson of Unit II.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Explain the Ethernet frame format" is the question — 5 to 10 marks. Draw the frame as a labelled box diagram with the byte count under every field, then one line per field. Then add the two derived facts that earn the extra marks: minimum frame 64 bytes (from the CSMA/CD round-trip rule) and maximum frame 1518 bytes. The generations table is a separate 3-mark question.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Network Layer: Functions and Services
sem.deck: What the network layer is responsible for, the difference between routing and forwarding, connectionless versus connection-oriented service, and the services this layer deliberately does not provide. The framing lesson for the whole of Unit III.
sem.oneIdea: What the network layer is responsible for, the difference between routing and forwarding, connectionless versus connection-oriented service, and the services this layer deliberately does not provide. The framing lesson for the whole of Unit III.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Asked as "Explain the functions/services of the network layer" — 5 marks. Structure it as packetizing, routing and forwarding as the three main duties, then the secondary ones. Keep two lines for routing vs forwarding, which is the sub-question most often used to separate answers, and one line for what IP does not provide — that omission is deliberate and examiners like to see it named.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: IP Addresses and Classful Addressing
sem.deck: The 32-bit IPv4 address, the five classes and how to recognise them instantly, the default masks, the special addresses, and the arithmetic for network address, broadcast address and host count. Everything in the next two lessons is built on this.
sem.oneIdea: The 32-bit IPv4 address, the five classes and how to recognise them instantly, the default masks, the special addresses, and the arithmetic for network address, broadcast address and host count. Everything in the next two lessons is built on this.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two questions, both mechanical. (1) "Explain classful addressing" — the five-class table with ranges, masks and host counts, 5 marks. (2) "Given the address X, find its class, network address, broadcast address and number of hosts" — pure arithmetic, and free marks once drilled. Memorise the first-byte ranges (1–126, 128–191, 192–223, 224–239, 240–255); with them, the class is identified in one second.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Classless Addressing (CIDR)
sem.deck: Slash notation, the three rules every block must obey, the mask table you should be able to write from memory, and the arithmetic for first address, last address and block size. This is the language subnetting is written in.
sem.oneIdea: Slash notation, the three rules every block must obey, the mask table you should be able to write from memory, and the arithmetic for first address, last address and block size. This is the language subnetting is written in.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

The question is almost always "Given the address a.b.c.d/n, find the first address, the last address and the number of addresses in the block" — 5 marks, entirely mechanical. Learn one formula and one table: block size = 2(32−n), and the /24 to /30 mask values. With those you never need to write binary at all.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Subnetting and VLSM
sem.deck: The highest marks-per-hour topic in the whole subject. Four worked numericals covering every shape the question takes: subnet-count based, host-count based, and a full VLSM allocation. Do not read this lesson — work it.
sem.oneIdea: The highest marks-per-hour topic in the whole subject. Four worked numericals covering every shape the question takes: subnet-count based, host-count based, and a full VLSM allocation. Do not read this lesson — work it.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Subnetting appears every year and is worth substantial marks. It is purely mechanical: there is nothing to understand once you have the procedure, only steps to execute without slipping. Always show the four lines — bits borrowed, new mask, block size, subnet table — because partial marks are awarded for each even if the arithmetic goes wrong later. And in a VLSM question, always allocate the largest requirement first; doing it in the order the question lists them is the single most common way to fail.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: The IPv4 Header and Fragmentation
sem.deck: Thirteen header fields with their sizes and purposes, then the fragmentation numerical — identification, flags and offset worked out fragment by fragment. A diagram question and a calculation question in one lesson.
sem.oneIdea: Thirteen header fields with their sizes and purposes, then the fragmentation numerical — identification, flags and offset worked out fragment by fragment. A diagram question and a calculation question in one lesson.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Draw and explain the IPv4 header" is a 10-mark near-certainty. Draw it as a grid four bytes (32 bits) wide, with the bit-width written under every field — that layout is itself worth marks because it shows why the header is a multiple of 4 bytes. Then one line per field. The fragmentation numerical is a separate 5-mark question; the three fields it turns on are identification, flags and fragmentation offset, so give those three extra attention.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: NAT, ARP and RARP
sem.deck: Three address-translation mechanisms. NAT maps private addresses to public ones; ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses; RARP does the reverse. Small topics, reliably asked, and easy marks once the directions are straight in your head.
sem.oneIdea: Three address-translation mechanisms. NAT maps private addresses to public ones; ARP maps IP addresses to MAC addresses; RARP does the reverse. Small topics, reliably asked, and easy marks once the directions are straight in your head.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Usually three separate short questions of 3–5 marks each. For NAT, draw the translation table — that diagram is most of the answer. For ARP, the marks are in the four-step process (broadcast request, unicast reply) and the ARP cache. The single most common error in the whole topic is reversing ARP and RARP, so fix the direction first: ARP goes IP → MAC.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: ICMP and IGMP
sem.deck: The two companion protocols of IP. ICMP reports errors and answers queries — it is what ping and traceroute are built from. IGMP manages multicast group membership. Both are descriptive, both are reliably asked, and both are short.
sem.oneIdea: The two companion protocols of IP. ICMP reports errors and answers queries — it is what ping and traceroute are built from. IGMP manages multicast group membership. Both are descriptive, both are reliably asked, and both are short.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Usually two 5-mark questions, or one 10-mark "explain ICMP and IGMP". For ICMP, structure the answer as error-reporting messages and query messages in two lists, then explain ping and traceroute — the applications are what make the answer concrete and they are frequently a sub-question in their own right. For IGMP, the three message types and the join/leave process carry the marks. Do not confuse the two: ICMP reports problems, IGMP manages groups.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Unicast and Multicast Routing
sem.deck: Distance vector and link state worked through with a real example, the count-to-infinity problem and its four fixes, RIP versus OSPF versus BGP, and then the multicast half — trees, RPF/RPB/RPM, and the three protocol families.
sem.oneIdea: Distance vector and link state worked through with a real example, the count-to-infinity problem and its four fixes, RIP versus OSPF versus BGP, and then the multicast half — trees, RPF/RPB/RPM, and the three protocol families.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two big questions. (1) "Compare distance vector and link state routing" — a table, plus a worked distance-vector iteration if the question gives a network. Show the table at each step; marks are awarded per iteration. (2) "Explain the count-to-infinity problem and its solutions" — the mechanism plus the four fixes. Multicast is usually a shorter 5-mark question: source-based versus group-shared tree and the three protocols.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: IPv6
sem.deck: 128-bit addresses, the abbreviation rules, the simplified 40-byte header, extension headers, the IPv4 versus IPv6 table, and the three transition strategies. The last lesson of Unit III.
sem.oneIdea: 128-bit addresses, the abbreviation rules, the simplified 40-byte header, extension headers, the IPv4 versus IPv6 table, and the three transition strategies. The last lesson of Unit III.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three questions live here, and all three are short. (1) "Compare IPv4 and IPv6" — a table of 8–10 rows, the most likely of the three. (2) "Draw and explain the IPv6 header" — only eight fields, so it is quicker than the IPv4 header question; make sure you can say which four fields were removed and why. (3) An abbreviation exercise — compress or expand an address; purely mechanical, and the ":: only once" rule is what is being tested.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Transport Layer: Introduction and Services
sem.deck: Process-to-process delivery, port numbers and socket addresses, multiplexing and demultiplexing, and the connectionless/connection-oriented split. The framing lesson for Unit IV.
sem.oneIdea: Process-to-process delivery, port numbers and socket addresses, multiplexing and demultiplexing, and the connectionless/connection-oriented split. The framing lesson for Unit IV.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Asked as "Explain the services of the transport layer" — 5 marks. Lead with the three deliveries line (hop-to-hop, host-to-host, process-to-process); it frames everything and takes one sentence. Then port addressing, multiplexing/demultiplexing, segmentation and reassembly, connection control, flow control, error control. The well-known port numbers are a separate one-mark question — learn the eight that matter.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: UDP — User Datagram Protocol
sem.deck: Eight bytes of header, four fields, and almost no services — and every one of those omissions is deliberate. The header, the pseudoheader checksum, the applications, and the TCP vs UDP table that is asked every year.
sem.oneIdea: Eight bytes of header, four fields, and almost no services — and every one of those omissions is deliberate. The header, the pseudoheader checksum, the applications, and the TCP vs UDP table that is asked every year.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Compare TCP and UDP" is the single most likely question in Unit IV — answer it as a table of 10–12 rows. "Draw the UDP header" is a 3-mark freebie: four fields, two bytes each, sixteen bytes total is wrong — it is eight. The sub-question that separates answers is "why would anyone use an unreliable protocol?", so have the applications list and the reasoning ready.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: TCP: Services and Header
sem.deck: Stream delivery, the numbering system that everything else depends on, the eleven header fields, the six control flags, and the options. The sequence-number rules in particular return in every remaining lesson of this unit.
sem.oneIdea: Stream delivery, the numbering system that everything else depends on, the eleven header fields, the six control flags, and the options. The sequence-number rules in particular return in every remaining lesson of this unit.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Draw and explain the TCP header" is a 10-mark near-certainty. Draw it four bytes (32 bits) per row with the bit-width under each field. The two places marks are actually lost: the six control flags (name all six, one line each) and the sequence vs acknowledgement number rule. Get those right and the rest is description.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: TCP Connection Management
sem.deck: The three-way handshake, data transfer, the four-way termination, half-close, and the state transition diagram. The handshake diagram alone is worth drawing until you can produce it in ninety seconds.
sem.oneIdea: The three-way handshake, data transfer, the four-way termination, half-close, and the state transition diagram. The handshake diagram alone is worth drawing until you can produce it in ninety seconds.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Explain TCP connection establishment and termination with a diagram" is a 10-mark question and among the most certain in the paper. Draw the timeline diagram — two vertical lines, arrows between them, each arrow labelled with its flags, seq and ack. That diagram carries most of the marks. Then the sub-questions: why three ways and not two, and why termination needs four.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: TCP Flow and Error Control
sem.deck: The sliding window in bytes rather than frames, the window-size formula that ties flow and congestion control together, silly window syndrome with both its fixes, and the three error-control mechanisms including fast retransmit.
sem.oneIdea: The sliding window in bytes rather than frames, the window-size formula that ties flow and congestion control together, silly window syndrome with both its fixes, and the three error-control mechanisms including fast retransmit.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two questions. (1) "Explain flow control in TCP" — draw the sliding window over a byte line, define the four pointers, and give the window-size formula. (2) "What is silly window syndrome and how is it solved?" — a 5-mark question with a clean structure: the sender's version fixed by Nagle's algorithm, the receiver's version fixed by Clark's solution or delayed acknowledgement. Naming the two algorithms is where the marks are.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: TCP Congestion Control
sem.deck: Slow start, congestion avoidance, congestion detection, and the difference between Tahoe and Reno — with a full window-by-window trace of the congestion window through a timeout and a fast retransmit.
sem.oneIdea: Slow start, congestion avoidance, congestion detection, and the difference between Tahoe and Reno — with a full window-by-window trace of the congestion window through a timeout and a fast retransmit.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Explain TCP congestion control with a diagram" is a 10-mark question and among the three most likely in Unit IV. Draw the cwnd-versus-time graph — exponential rise, the ssthresh line, linear rise, the drop — and label every phase on it. Then trace the numbers in a table. The Tahoe vs Reno distinction is the sub-question that separates good answers, so keep two rows for it.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: TCP Timers, Options and SCTP
sem.deck: The four timers with the RTO calculation worked out, the seven TCP options, and SCTP — its two headline features, its cookie handshake, and the three-way comparison that closes Unit IV.
sem.oneIdea: The four timers with the RTO calculation worked out, the seven TCP options, and SCTP — its two headline features, its cookie handshake, and the three-way comparison that closes Unit IV.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three short questions rather than one long one. "Explain TCP timers" — name all four with one line each, 4 marks. "What is Karn's algorithm?" — 3 marks, and it needs the problem stated before the fix. "Explain SCTP / compare TCP, UDP and SCTP" — 5 marks, and multi-homing and multi-streaming are the two words that must appear.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: The Application Layer and Client-Server Model
sem.deck: The paradigms applications are built on, the socket interface, and the map of which protocol sits on which transport and port. Short, but it organises the seven lessons that follow.
sem.oneIdea: The paradigms applications are built on, the socket interface, and the map of which protocol sits on which transport and port. Short, but it organises the seven lessons that follow.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Rarely a question on its own — more often the opening paragraph of a longer application-layer answer, and the source of one-mark questions about ports and paradigms. The two things genuinely worth memorising: the client-server vs P2P table (which also appeared in Unit I, so it is free marks twice), and the protocol/transport/port table at the end of this lesson.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: DNS — Domain Name System
sem.deck: The namespace, zones and servers, the two resolution methods, caching, and the resource record types. The recursive-versus-iterative diagram is the single most-drawn figure in Unit V.
sem.oneIdea: The namespace, zones and servers, the two resolution methods, caching, and the resource record types. The recursive-versus-iterative diagram is the single most-drawn figure in Unit V.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Explain DNS with the resolution process" is a 10-mark near-certainty. Structure it as: what DNS is → the namespace diagram (an inverted tree) → the server hierarchy → recursive and iterative resolution, drawn as two separate diagrams → caching. The two diagrams are where the marks are; the difference between them is the sub-question that separates answers.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: DHCP — Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol
sem.deck: The DORA sequence, the four items a host receives, leases and renewal, and the relay agent that lets one server cover many networks. A short lesson with one diagram that must be drawn correctly.
sem.oneIdea: The DORA sequence, the four items a host receives, leases and renewal, and the relay agent that lets one server cover many networks. A short lesson with one diagram that must be drawn correctly.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

A 5-mark question, and the marks are concentrated in one place: the DORA sequence, drawn as a four-arrow timeline with the message names labelled. Learn the acronym, learn which two messages are broadcast and why, and add the relay agent in one line — that last point is what separates a 5 from a 3.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: FTP, TELNET and SSH
sem.deck: FTP's two connections and the active/passive distinction, TELNET's network virtual terminal, and why SSH replaced it. Two protocols named in the syllabus, and the third because no answer about TELNET is complete without it.
sem.oneIdea: FTP's two connections and the active/passive distinction, TELNET's network virtual terminal, and why SSH replaced it. Two protocols named in the syllabus, and the third because no answer about TELNET is complete without it.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Explain FTP with a diagram" is a 5-mark question, and the diagram must show two connections, not one — that is the whole point of FTP and the single fact examiners check. For TELNET, the marks are in the Network Virtual Terminal concept and in why TELNET is insecure. Keep two lines for SSH as the answer to that.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: WWW and HTTP
sem.deck: URLs, the three kinds of web document, the HTTP request and response formats, the methods and status codes, persistent versus non-persistent connections with a worked timing comparison, and cookies and caching.
sem.oneIdea: URLs, the three kinds of web document, the HTTP request and response formats, the methods and status codes, persistent versus non-persistent connections with a worked timing comparison, and cookies and caching.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two questions. (1) "Explain HTTP with its message format" — draw the request and response formats as labelled blocks, then the methods and status-code classes. (2) "Differentiate persistent and non-persistent HTTP" — a short comparison, and the marks are in the RTT count, so learn the two formulas. Cookies are a standard 3-mark add-on: HTTP is stateless, cookies are how state is added on top.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Electronic Mail
sem.deck: The three components, the push-versus-pull split that explains why three protocols are needed, SMTP, POP3 and IMAP4, and MIME. The last application-layer lesson before the security half.
sem.oneIdea: The three components, the push-versus-pull split that explains why three protocols are needed, SMTP, POP3 and IMAP4, and MIME. The last application-layer lesson before the security half.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

"Explain the architecture of e-mail" or "Compare SMTP, POP3 and IMAP" — 5 to 10 marks. The single insight that organises the whole answer is push versus pull: SMTP pushes, POP and IMAP pull. Draw the sender-to-receiver diagram showing where each protocol operates, and the answer writes itself. MIME is a separate 3-mark question — know what problem it solves.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: Network Security Fundamentals and Cryptography
sem.deck: The security goals, the attacks against each, symmetric versus asymmetric cryptography, and RSA worked end to end with real numbers. The one numerical in the security half of this syllabus.
sem.oneIdea: The security goals, the attacks against each, symmetric versus asymmetric cryptography, and RSA worked end to end with real numbers. The one numerical in the security half of this syllabus.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three questions. (1) "Explain the goals of security and the attacks that threaten them" — organise the attacks under the goals rather than as a flat list; that structure is worth marks by itself. (2) "Compare symmetric and asymmetric cryptography" — a table. (3) An RSA numerical — the only calculation in this half, and entirely mechanical once you can do modular exponentiation.

sem.subject: Computer Networks
sem.title: SSL, IPsec, Firewalls and Intrusion Detection
sem.deck: Security applied at three different layers, and the two defensive devices. Where each mechanism sits in the stack is the organising idea of the whole lesson — and the last lesson of the syllabus.
sem.oneIdea: Security applied at three different layers, and the two defensive devices. Where each mechanism sits in the stack is the organising idea of the whole lesson — and the last lesson of the syllabus.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Usually two or three short questions rather than one long one. "Compare SSL and IPsec" — and the answer starts with which layer each operates at, because everything else follows from that. "Explain types of firewall" — packet filter versus proxy, with the layer each works at. "Explain IDS and its types" — two classifications, by placement and by detection method; giving both is what distinguishes a full answer.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Language Processors
sem.deck: What a translator is, compiler versus interpreter, the complete language-processing system from preprocessor to loader, the hybrid model that Java uses, and the six kinds of translator worth naming.
sem.oneIdea: What a translator is, compiler versus interpreter, the complete language-processing system from preprocessor to loader, the hybrid model that Java uses, and the six kinds of translator worth naming.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two questions live here and both are certain. “Differentiate compiler and interpreter” — an eight-row table, and the winning row is where the error is reported. “Explain the language processing system with a diagram” — draw the vertical chain source → preprocessor → compiler → assembler → linker/loader → machine code and label what flows between each pair; the diagram alone carries most of the marks. Learn the hybrid Java model too, because it is the natural follow-up question and it sets up just-in-time compilation in Lesson 4.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: The Structure of a Compiler — the Six Phases
sem.deck: Every phase with its input, output and the errors it catches, the whole sequence traced on one real statement, the symbol table and error handler that run alongside, and the difference between a phase and a pass.
sem.oneIdea: Every phase with its input, output and the errors it catches, the whole sequence traced on one real statement, the symbol table and error handler that run alongside, and the difference between a phase and a pass.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain the phases of a compiler with a diagram, showing the translation of a statement” is the most-asked question in this entire paper. It is worth 10 marks and it is the same question every year. The answer has a fixed shape: draw the vertical phase diagram with the symbol table and error handler beside it, then trace position = initial + rate * 60 through all six phases, writing the output of each phase. Learn that trace by heart — the token stream, the syntax tree, the three-address code, the optimised code and the assembly. Also learn phase vs pass, a standard 2-marker.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Compiler Construction Tools, Language Evolution, and Applications
sem.deck: The six kinds of compiler-writing tool and which phase each builds, the five generations of programming language with the two great classifications, and the five areas where compiler technology is used outside compilers.
sem.oneIdea: The six kinds of compiler-writing tool and which phase each builds, the five generations of programming language with the two great classifications, and the five areas where compiler technology is used outside compilers.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three separate short-answer topics in one lesson, and each is a clean 5-marker. “List and explain compiler construction tools” — six tools, and the mark is in naming which phase each one generates and its input formalism. “Explain the evolution of programming languages” — five generations with examples, plus the imperative/declarative and static/dynamic scoping distinctions. “Applications of compiler technology” — five headings; this is the high-yield question students regularly skip. Prepare all three in full.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Transition Diagrams, Bootstrapping and Just-in-Time Compilation
sem.deck: The notation and conventions of transition diagrams, bootstrapping with T-diagrams worked through the full three-step cross-compiler problem, and how just-in-time compilation recovers the speed that interpretation gives away.
sem.oneIdea: The notation and conventions of transition diagrams, bootstrapping with T-diagrams worked through the full three-step cross-compiler problem, and how just-in-time compilation recovers the speed that interpretation gives away.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Bootstrapping is the premier examinable question here — “What is bootstrapping? Explain with T-diagrams” is a recurring 5–10 mark question, and examiners expect the full three-step cross-compiler construction worked below. Draw every T-diagram with its source, target, and implementation arms clearly labelled. Transition diagrams require knowing the four conventions — above all the retract asterisk (*). JIT compilation is tested as a short note or 3-way comparison table against AOT compilation and interpretation.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: The Role of the Lexical Analyser
sem.deck: Tokens, patterns and lexemes kept apart, the attributes a token carries, why lexical analysis is separated from parsing at all, token-counting numericals, and lexical errors with their four recovery strategies.
sem.oneIdea: Tokens, patterns and lexemes kept apart, the attributes a token carries, why lexical analysis is separated from parsing at all, token-counting numericals, and lexical errors with their four recovery strategies.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Define token, pattern and lexeme with examples” is a guaranteed 2–5 marker, and the marks are lost by students who cannot keep the three apart — so learn the one-line test below. “Why is lexical analysis separated from syntax analysis?” has exactly three reasons and they are worth memorising as three words: simplicity, efficiency, portability. Token-counting numericals appear in objective sections constantly and are free marks once you know that a string literal is one token. Lexical error recovery is a standard 4-mark list.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Input Buffering
sem.deck: Why the scanner needs lookahead, the one-buffer scheme and where it breaks, buffer pairs with their two pointers and the reload algorithm, and the sentinel trick that halves the tests per character — with the arithmetic to prove it.
sem.oneIdea: Why the scanner needs lookahead, the one-buffer scheme and where it breaks, buffer pairs with their two pointers and the reload algorithm, and the sentinel trick that halves the tests per character — with the arithmetic to prove it.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain input buffering with sentinels” is a reliable 5–10 mark question, and it has a fixed shape: state why buffering is needed, draw the two-buffer diagram with lexemeBegin and forward marked, give the code before and after sentinels, and finish with “two tests per character become one”.
