That last sentence is the point of the whole topic and the one students omit. The eof sentinel character and the reason N is the disk block size are the two details examiners probe.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Specification of Tokens
sem.deck: Alphabets, strings and languages with the counting formulas, the four operations on languages, regular expressions with their precedence and algebraic laws, regular definitions for real tokens, and ten worked “write the regular expression” problems.
sem.oneIdea: Alphabets, strings and languages with the counting formulas, the four operations on languages, regular expressions with their precedence and algebraic laws, regular definitions for real tokens, and ten worked “write the regular expression” problems.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three question shapes, all mechanical. “Write a regular expression for …” — ten worked below, and the patterns repeat; learn the four templates in the box before them. “Give the regular definition for identifiers and numbers” — write it exactly as Aho does, since that is what the examiner has in front of him. “Define alphabet, string, language, prefix, suffix, substring” — a 5-mark definitions question, with the counting formulas as a likely objective follow-up. Everything here feeds Lesson 8, where these expressions become automata.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Recognition of Tokens — Transition Diagrams, NFA and the Subset Construction
sem.deck: Transition diagrams for real tokens, finite automata compared, Thompson's construction from a regular expression to an NFA, and the subset construction from NFA to DFA — both worked in full on (a|b)*abb.
sem.oneIdea: Transition diagrams for real tokens, finite automata compared, Thompson's construction from a regular expression to an NFA, and the subset construction from NFA to DFA — both worked in full on (a|b)*abb.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

This is the highest-value lesson in Unit II, and it is entirely mechanical. Two guaranteed questions: “Convert the given regular expression to an NFA using Thompson's construction” and “Convert the NFA to a DFA using the subset construction” — often as one question in two parts on the same expression. The marks are in the working: number every NFA state, and for the subset construction show the ε-closure of every set you form and lay the answer out as a transition table with named states A, B, C… Learn (a|b)*abb by heart — it is the example in Aho, so it is the example your examiner will set.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: DFA Minimisation and the Direct RE → DFA Method
sem.deck: Minimising a DFA by partitioning, worked to completion on the machine from Lesson 8; then the direct route from regular expression to DFA using a syntax tree with nullable, firstpos, lastpos and followpos — with both answers cross-checked against each other.
sem.oneIdea: Minimising a DFA by partitioning, worked to completion on the machine from Lesson 8; then the direct route from regular expression to DFA using a syntax tree with nullable, firstpos, lastpos and followpos — with both answers cross-checked against each other.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two more guaranteed, mechanical questions. “Minimise the given DFA” — the answer is a sequence of partitions Π0, Π1, Π2 … and you must show every partition and say which state split the group and why. “Construct a DFA directly from the regular expression” — draw the syntax tree with numbered leaves, build the nullable / firstpos / lastpos table, then the followpos table, then the DFA. The followpos table is where the marks are. Both methods are worked here on (a|b)*abb, and they are shown to agree — which is the best possible check on your own answer.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Lex — the Lexical Analyser Generator
sem.deck: The three-part structure of a Lex program, a complete worked specification, the variables and functions you must name, the two conflict-resolution rules with traces, and how Lex builds its automaton internally.
sem.oneIdea: The three-part structure of a Lex program, a complete worked specification, the variables and functions you must name, the two conflict-resolution rules with traces, and how Lex builds its automaton internally.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain the structure of a Lex program” is the certain question — three sections separated by %%, and you should write a small complete specification rather than describe one. “How does Lex resolve conflicts?” has exactly two rules, in order: longest match first, then earliest rule listed — and the if versus ifx example proves you understand both. “How does Lex work internally?” ties this lesson back to Lessons 8 and 9, which is the answer examiners reward. Learn yytext, yyleng, yylex(), yywrap() by name.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Context-Free Grammars and Syntax Specification
sem.deck: Formal definition of CFGs, derivations and parse trees, proving grammar ambiguity, eliminating immediate and indirect left recursion, and left factoring for predictive parsing.
sem.oneIdea: Formal definition of CFGs, derivations and parse trees, proving grammar ambiguity, eliminating immediate and indirect left recursion, and left factoring for predictive parsing.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Prove that the given grammar is ambiguous” is a guaranteed 5-mark university question: draw two distinct parse trees (or provide two different leftmost derivations) for the exact same input string. “Eliminate left recursion” is another guaranteed 5–10 marker — know both immediate left recursion and the systematic algorithm for indirect left recursion. “Left factor the grammar” is required to prepare grammars for top-down LL(1) predictive parsing.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Recursive Descent Parsing
sem.deck: Top-down parsing mechanics, recursive procedures for each non-terminal, the problem of backtracking, and how predictive grammars eliminate trial-and-error parsing.
sem.oneIdea: Top-down parsing mechanics, recursive procedures for each non-terminal, the problem of backtracking, and how predictive grammars eliminate trial-and-error parsing.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Write a recursive descent parser for the given grammar” is a common 5–10 mark university question. Examiners look for: one procedure per non-terminal, a working match() helper function that advances the input lookahead pointer, explicit handling of ε-productions (do nothing), and error reporting. You must also be able to explain why backtracking is inefficient and how LL(1) grammars eliminate it.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Predictive Parsing — FIRST, FOLLOW and LL(1)
sem.deck: Computing FIRST and FOLLOW sets, building the LL(1) parsing table, formal conditions for LL(1) grammars, and stack-driven predictive parsing with complete trace.
sem.oneIdea: Computing FIRST and FOLLOW sets, building the LL(1) parsing table, formal conditions for LL(1) grammars, and stack-driven predictive parsing with complete trace.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

This is the highest-scoring topic in Unit III. “Compute FIRST and FOLLOW sets” is a guaranteed 10-mark question. “Construct the LL(1) parsing table and parse the string id + id * id” is a 10–15 mark numerical. Examiners grade on: showing the computation for every non-terminal, correct end-marker $ in FOLLOW(S), no duplicate entries in table cells, and a full three-column stack trace table.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Bottom-Up Parsing — Shift-Reduce
sem.deck: Bottom-up parsing principles, handles and handle pruning, the four parser actions, shift-reduce conflicts, and a complete stack trace on arithmetic expressions.
sem.oneIdea: Bottom-up parsing principles, handles and handle pruning, the four parser actions, shift-reduce conflicts, and a complete stack trace on arithmetic expressions.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Define handle and handle pruning with an example” is a guaranteed 5-marker. “Explain the four actions of a shift-reduce parser and its conflicts” (Shift/Reduce and Reduce/Reduce) is another guaranteed question. “Trace the parsing of a string using shift-reduce parsing” requires a 4-column table: Stack, Input Buffer, Action Taken, and Handle Identified.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Simple LR (SLR) Parsing
sem.deck: LR(0) items, the canonical collection of item sets, closure and GOTO operations, constructing the SLR(1) parsing table using FOLLOW sets, step-by-step stack simulation, and SLR conflict detection.
sem.oneIdea: LR(0) items, the canonical collection of item sets, closure and GOTO operations, constructing the SLR(1) parsing table using FOLLOW sets, step-by-step stack simulation, and SLR conflict detection.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Construct the SLR parsing table for the given grammar and trace the string” is a 15–20 mark master question in almost every university paper. To score full marks: (1) state the augmented grammar, (2) compute CLOSURE and GOTO for every item set $I_0 \dots I_n$, (3) draw the DFA state transition diagram, (4) calculate FOLLOW sets for all non-terminals, (5) write the SLR(1) Action & Goto table, and (6) execute the complete 4-column stack simulation table.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: CLR(1) and LALR(1) Parsing
sem.deck: LR(1) items with context lookahead, canonical LR (CLR) table construction, merging same-core states into LALR(1), conflict behavior during state merging, and the master comparison hierarchy.
sem.oneIdea: LR(1) items with context lookahead, canonical LR (CLR) table construction, merging same-core states into LALR(1), conflict behavior during state merging, and the master comparison hierarchy.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Construct the CLR and LALR parsing tables for the given grammar” carries 15–20 marks and is the most mathematically demanding question in Unit III. You must: (1) clearly define an LR(1) item $[A \to \alpha \cdot \beta, a]$, (2) compute the 10-state canonical LR(1) collection, (3) demonstrate how states with identical cores merge into the 7-state LALR(1) collection, and (4) reproduce the 5-point comparison table across LR(0), SLR(1), LALR(1), and CLR(1).

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Parser Generators — Yacc & Bison
sem.deck: Yacc/Bison architecture, the Lex–Yacc cooperative pipeline, three-section program structure, semantic attribute binding ($$, $1, $2), operator precedence directives, conflict resolution rules, and error recovery.
sem.oneIdea: Yacc/Bison architecture, the Lex–Yacc cooperative pipeline, three-section program structure, semantic attribute binding ($$, $1, $2), operator precedence directives, conflict resolution rules, and error recovery.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain the structure of a Yacc program with an example” is a guaranteed 10–15 mark question. “How does Yacc resolve Shift/Reduce and Reduce/Reduce conflicts?” and “Draw the Lex-Yacc cooperative communication diagram” are frequent 5-markers. Provide the exact three-section layout, describe %token, %left, %right, and write a clean calculator example.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Syntax-Directed Translation — SDD and SDT
sem.deck: Syntax-Directed Definitions (SDDs), synthesised and inherited attributes, dependency graphs, annotated parse trees, S-attributed vs L-attributed definitions, and Syntax-Directed Translation Schemes (SDTs).
sem.oneIdea: Syntax-Directed Definitions (SDDs), synthesised and inherited attributes, dependency graphs, annotated parse trees, S-attributed vs L-attributed definitions, and Syntax-Directed Translation Schemes (SDTs).
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Differentiate between synthesised and inherited attributes with examples” is a guaranteed 5-mark question. “Compare S-attributed and L-attributed definitions” is another staple. “Draw the annotated parse tree and dependency graph for an expression” carries 10 marks. Be prepared to show the bottom-up flow of synthesised values versus the top-down/left-to-right flow of inherited values.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Intermediate Code Generation — Three-Address Code
sem.deck: Intermediate representations, the eight instruction forms of Three-Address Code (TAC), quadruples, triples, indirect triples, and optimization trade-offs with worked translation matrices.
sem.oneIdea: Intermediate representations, the eight instruction forms of Three-Address Code (TAC), quadruples, triples, indirect triples, and optimization trade-offs with worked translation matrices.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Generate Three-Address Code, Quadruples, and Triples for the given expression” is a guaranteed 10–15 mark question. “Compare Quadruples, Triples, and Indirect Triples with respect to instruction reordering” is a frequent 5-marker. Always write the TAC statement list first, label temporaries clearly ($t_1, t_2, \dots$), and construct clean side-by-side tables.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Translation of Declarations, Expressions, and Type Checking
sem.deck: Syntax-directed generation of Three-Address Code for arithmetic expressions, 1D and 2D array address formulas (Row-Major vs Column-Major), short-circuit boolean evaluation, and control flow constructs.
sem.oneIdea: Syntax-directed generation of Three-Address Code for arithmetic expressions, 1D and 2D array address formulas (Row-Major vs Column-Major), short-circuit boolean evaluation, and control flow constructs.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Derive the address calculation formula for a 2D array in Row-Major and Column-Major order and generate TAC” is a 10–15 mark numerical question. “Generate Three-Address Code for an if-else or while loop with short-circuit evaluation” is a frequent 10-marker. Show compile-time constant offsets ($C$) clearly and label all jump destinations.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Control Flow Translation — Backpatching
sem.deck: The forward-jump dilemma in single-pass compilers, the backpatching technique, makelist, merge, and backpatch primitives, SDD rules for boolean expressions and control structures, with a fully worked quad trace.
sem.oneIdea: The forward-jump dilemma in single-pass compilers, the backpatching technique, makelist, merge, and backpatch primitives, SDD rules for boolean expressions and control structures, with a fully worked quad trace.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain the backpatching technique with functions makelist, merge, and backpatch” is a standard 10-marker. “Translate a given boolean expression and if-else / while statement using backpatching” is a frequent 15-mark numerical. State the marker non-terminals $M$ and $N$, write the emitted quad table with blanks, and trace list merges and backpatch steps explicitly.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Runtime Environment — Activation Records & Storage
sem.deck: Memory layout, activation trees, the seven fields of an activation record, static vs stack vs heap allocation, dynamic vs static links, and parameter passing mechanisms (Value, Reference, Value-Result, Name).
sem.oneIdea: Memory layout, activation trees, the seven fields of an activation record, static vs stack vs heap allocation, dynamic vs static links, and parameter passing mechanisms (Value, Reference, Value-Result, Name).
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Draw and explain the structure of an Activation Record (stack frame)” is a guaranteed 7–10 marker. “Compare Static, Stack, and Heap storage allocation strategies” is another frequent 10-marker. “Trace a program under Call-by-Value, Call-by-Reference, and Call-by-Value-Result” is a classic numerical problem where aliasing causes different outputs. Know all 7 fields of the activation record by heart.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Sources of Optimization
sem.deck: Classification of compiler optimizations, function-preserving transformations, common subexpression elimination, copy propagation, dead-code elimination, constant folding, and loop-invariant code motion.
sem.oneIdea: Classification of compiler optimizations, function-preserving transformations, common subexpression elimination, copy propagation, dead-code elimination, constant folding, and loop-invariant code motion.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain the principal sources of optimization with suitable examples” is a recurring 10-mark question. Clearly separate function-preserving transformations from loop transformations and illustrate each with concise 3-address code fragments.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Basic Blocks and Flow Graphs
sem.deck: Partitioning intermediate code into basic blocks using the leader algorithm, constructing control-flow graphs (CFGs), loop identification, and predecessor/successor relationships.
sem.oneIdea: Partitioning intermediate code into basic blocks using the leader algorithm, constructing control-flow graphs (CFGs), loop identification, and predecessor/successor relationships.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Partition the given 3-address code into basic blocks and draw the control flow graph” is a guaranteed 7-to-10 mark numerical. Examiners grade on: (1) clearly listing the three leader rules, (2) identifying every leader by statement number, (3) block boundaries, and (4) properly directed edges including back-edges.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: DAG Representation and Local Optimization
sem.deck: Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) construction for basic blocks, value numbering, detecting local common subexpressions, dead code elimination, and algebraic identities.
sem.oneIdea: Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) construction for basic blocks, value numbering, detecting local common subexpressions, dead code elimination, and algebraic identities.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Construct the DAG for the given basic block and write the optimized three-address code” is one of the most frequently asked problems in compiler design. Show the step-by-step node creation, attach variable names to nodes, demonstrate subexpression sharing, and write out the resulting streamlined code.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Data-Flow Analysis and Loop Optimization
sem.deck: The data-flow abstraction, transfer equations (Gen and Kill), reaching definitions, available expressions, live variables, dominator trees, and natural loop optimization.
sem.oneIdea: The data-flow abstraction, transfer equations (Gen and Kill), reaching definitions, available expressions, live variables, dominator trees, and natural loop optimization.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Compare Reaching Definitions, Available Expressions, and Live Variables” is a guaranteed 8-to-10 mark theory question. Always draw the 4-quadrant comparison table showing: direction (forward/backward), meet operator ($\cup$ / $\cap$), boundary condition, and optimization enabled.

sem.subject: Compiler Design
sem.title: Code Generation and Peephole Optimization
sem.deck: Design issues in target code generation, register allocation and assignment, global register allocation via graph coloring (Chaitin's heuristic), and peephole optimization techniques.
sem.oneIdea: Design issues in target code generation, register allocation and assignment, global register allocation via graph coloring (Chaitin's heuristic), and peephole optimization techniques.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“What is peephole optimization? Explain its characteristics with examples” is a guaranteed 5-mark question in almost every university paper. “Explain register allocation via graph coloring” is the standard 7-to-10 mark question on the final phase of compilation.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: The RAM Model and the Analysis of Algorithms
sem.deck: What an algorithm is and the five properties it must have, the RAM model of computation, counting primitive operations, best, worst and average case, space complexity, and the a priori–a posteriori distinction.
sem.oneIdea: What an algorithm is and the five properties it must have, the RAM model of computation, counting primitive operations, best, worst and average case, space complexity, and the a priori–a posteriori distinction.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

This lesson is definition marks and the foundation for everything after it. Two questions recur: “Define an algorithm and state its characteristics” (5 marks — five properties, one line each) and “What is the RAM model? Why is it used?”. The frequency-count table below is the technique every complexity question in Lesson 3 uses, so learn it here properly rather than fighting it later. Best/worst/average case for linear search and quick sort is a near-certain short answer.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Asymptotic Notations and Their Significance
sem.deck: The formal definitions of O, Ω, Θ, little-o and little-ω, ten worked proofs finding c and n 0 , the growth-rate ordering, the properties, and the comparison table.
sem.oneIdea: The formal definitions of O, Ω, Θ, little-o and little-ω, ten worked proofs finding c and n 0 , the growth-rate ordering, the properties, and the comparison table.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

This is the most reliably examined topic in Unit I. Three shapes: “Define big oh, omega and theta with graphs” (draw all three graphs — they are worth a mark each); “Show that 3n + 2 = O(n)” (you must produce actual values of c and n0, not wave at the definition); and “Arrange these functions in increasing order of growth”. Memorise the growth-rate chain below — it answers the third shape instantly and helps in every recurrence question later.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Complexity Analysis of Algorithms
sem.deck: The four rules for reading complexity off code, then twenty worked fragments — simple loops, dependent loops, multiplying and dividing counters, the harmonic-series case, the √n cases, and recursion.
sem.oneIdea: The four rules for reading complexity off code, then twenty worked fragments — simple loops, dependent loops, multiplying and dividing counters, the harmonic-series case, the √n cases, and recursion.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Find the time complexity of the following code” is worth 2–5 marks and appears in every paper, often three times over. It is pure pattern recognition — there are only about eight distinct patterns, and they are all below. Learn to spot the counter's update rule first: i++ gives n, i = i*2 gives log n, i = i+i also gives log n, i*i ≤ n gives √n, and j = j+i inside an i-loop gives n log n. Everything else is those five combined.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Recurrence Relations
sem.deck: The three methods — back-substitution (iteration), the recursion tree, and substitution with induction — worked through twelve recurrences, plus the change-of-variable trick.
sem.oneIdea: The three methods — back-substitution (iteration), the recursion tree, and substitution with induction — worked through twelve recurrences, plus the change-of-variable trick.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Solve the recurrence T(n) = … using the substitution method / recursion tree method” is a 5–10 mark question, and it appears every year. Read the wording carefully: if it names a method, you must use that method — quoting the Master theorem earns nothing. Learn the back-substitution discipline below: expand exactly three times, spot the pattern, write the general k-th term, then set k so the recursion bottoms out. That is the whole technique, and it never fails.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Master's Theorem
sem.deck: The three cases for dividing functions with the extended fourth case, twenty drilled recurrences, the master theorem for decreasing functions, and the five situations where it does not apply.
sem.oneIdea: The three cases for dividing functions with the extended fourth case, twenty drilled recurrences, the master theorem for decreasing functions, and the five situations where it does not apply.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

These are the cheapest marks in the whole subject. A Master-theorem question is two lines of work: identify a, b and k, compare a with bk, write the answer. Expect two or three of them per paper, sometimes as objective questions. Drill the twenty below until identification is instant — and learn the decreasing-function version too, because syllabi that name “Master's theorem” separately, as this one does, usually examine both.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Introduction to the Algorithmic Paradigms
sem.deck: Divide and conquer, greedy, backtracking and branch and bound — the control abstraction of each, one fully worked example apiece, and the comparison table that answers “differentiate” questions.
sem.oneIdea: Divide and conquer, greedy, backtracking and branch and bound — the control abstraction of each, one fully worked example apiece, and the comparison table that answers “differentiate” questions.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

The syllabus says “basic introduction to algorithmic paradigms” — so Unit I asks you to describe and compare them, not to solve large instances. Units III and IV do that. The two question shapes here are “explain the divide-and-conquer / greedy / backtracking strategy with an example” and “differentiate backtracking and branch and bound” — which is by far the most-asked comparison in the whole subject. Learn the four control abstractions and the two comparison tables, and one worked example each.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Binary Search Trees
sem.deck: The BST property, construction from a key sequence, the three traversals, the three deletion cases worked in full, reconstructing a tree from two traversals, and why an unbalanced BST degenerates to a linked list.
sem.oneIdea: The BST property, construction from a key sequence, the three traversals, the three deletion cases worked in full, reconstructing a tree from two traversals, and why an unbalanced BST degenerates to a linked list.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three question shapes, all mechanical. “Construct a BST from the following keys and give its traversals” — draw the tree neatly, then read off all three traversals; the inorder must come out sorted, which is your free self-check. “Delete key X and redraw” — the three cases, and the two-child case is the one that gets marked. “Construct the tree from the given inorder and preorder” — a standard 5-marker. Everything in Lessons 8–10 is built on this lesson, so get it solid first.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: AVL Trees
sem.deck: The balance factor, the four rotations with the rule for picking the right one, a full six-key insertion trace, deletion with its R0/R1/R−1 cases, and the minimum-nodes recurrence that bounds the height.
sem.oneIdea: The balance factor, the four rotations with the rule for picking the right one, a full six-key insertion trace, deletion with its R0/R1/R−1 cases, and the minimum-nodes recurrence that bounds the height.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Construct an AVL tree by inserting the following keys, showing all rotations” is a 10-mark question and appears constantly. Three things earn the marks: write the balance factor beside every node after every insertion; name the rotation (LL, RR, LR, RL) before performing it; and redraw the tree after each rotation, not just at the end. The minimum-nodes recurrence N(h) = N(h−1) + N(h−2) + 1 is a separate short question worth memorising outright.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Red–Black Trees
sem.deck: The five properties, the height bound and why it holds, the three insertion cases with a seven-key worked trace, the double-black deletion cases, and the AVL comparison.
sem.oneIdea: The five properties, the height bound and why it holds, the three insertion cases with a seven-key worked trace, the double-black deletion cases, and the AVL comparison.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two questions. “State the properties of a red–black tree and insert the following keys” — write the five properties verbatim first (they are worth marks on their own), then trace the insertion, naming the case at every fix-up. “Compare AVL and red–black trees” — the table at the end. Learn the height bound h ≤ 2 log2(n+1) and the one-line reason for it. Deletion is examined far less often than insertion; know the vocabulary and the four cases, but drill insertion.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: B-Trees and B+ Trees
sem.deck: Why disks need a different tree, the order rules, insertion by splitting, deletion by borrowing and merging, the height bounds, and the B-tree versus B+ tree comparison.
sem.oneIdea: Why disks need a different tree, the order rules, insertion by splitting, deletion by borrowing and merging, the height bounds, and the B-tree versus B+ tree comparison.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Construct a B-tree of order m by inserting the following keys” is the question, and it is entirely mechanical once you know two numbers: max keys = m − 1 and min keys = ⌈m/2⌉ − 1. Write both numbers at the top of your answer before you start. Redraw the tree after every split — the marks are in the intermediate states. Deletion is asked less often but follows one rule: borrow if a sibling can spare a key, otherwise merge. B-tree vs B+ tree is a reliable short comparison.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Hashing and Collision Resolution
sem.deck: The four hash functions, chaining and the three open-addressing schemes with the same key set worked through all of them, the load factor, the probe-count formulas, clustering, and rehashing.
sem.oneIdea: The four hash functions, chaining and the three open-addressing schemes with the same key set worked through all of them, the load factor, the probe-count formulas, clustering, and rehashing.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

The guaranteed question is “Insert the following keys into a hash table of size m using linear probing / quadratic probing / double hashing” — often two of the three on the same key set, so you can compare. Draw the table as numbered slots and fill them in order, showing every probe you rejected. Then: “Differentiate open hashing and closed hashing”, and “Define load factor and primary clustering”. Learn the probe-count formulas — a numerical on them appears surprisingly often and almost nobody prepares it.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Heaps and Priority Queues
sem.deck: The heap property, the array representation and its index formulas, heapify, the O(n) build-heap proof, insertion and extraction, the counting formulas, and what a priority queue is used for.
sem.oneIdea: The heap property, the array representation and its index formulas, heapify, the O(n) build-heap proof, insertion and extraction, the counting formulas, and what a priority queue is used for.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two questions, both certain. “Build a max-heap from the given array” — work bottom-up from index ⌊n/2⌋, and show the array after every heapify call. “Prove that build-heap runs in O(n) time” — a 5-mark derivation that most students cannot do, so it is worth learning outright; the whole proof is the sum Σ h/2h = 2. Also learn the index formulas and the counting formulas (leaves, internal nodes, height), which appear as objective questions.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Comparison-Based Sorting
sem.deck: Merge sort, quick sort and heap sort — each traced in full, each analysed by recurrence in the best, average and worst case — plus the decision-tree proof that no comparison sort can beat n log n.
sem.oneIdea: Merge sort, quick sort and heap sort — each traced in full, each analysed by recurrence in the best, average and worst case — plus the decision-tree proof that no comparison sort can beat n log n.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

This is the highest-value lesson in Unit II. Four questions recur: “Sort the following array using merge sort / quick sort / heap sort, showing all steps”; “Derive the worst-case and average-case complexity of quick sort” (a 10-marker — write the recurrence, then solve it); “Compare the sorting algorithms” (the table at the end); and “Prove the Ω(n log n) lower bound” (the decision-tree argument, worth 5 marks and rarely prepared). Learn all four.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Sorting in Linear Time
sem.deck: Counting sort with the cumulative-count table worked cell by cell, radix sort pass by pass, bucket sort, why none of them contradicts the Ω(n log n) bound, and when each is actually usable.
sem.oneIdea: Counting sort with the cumulative-count table worked cell by cell, radix sort pass by pass, bucket sort, why none of them contradicts the Ω(n log n) bound, and when each is actually usable.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Sort the following using counting sort / radix sort, showing all intermediate arrays” is the question, and it is entirely mechanical. Two things earn the marks: show the count array before and after the cumulative step, and show every pass of radix sort as a separate line. The companion theory question is “How do these algorithms beat the Ω(n log n) lower bound?” — the answer is one sentence, given below, and it is worth learning exactly.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: String Matching — KMP and Boyer–Moore
sem.deck: The naive algorithm and why it is slow, the KMP failure function computed cell by cell with a full trace, Boyer–Moore's bad-character and good-suffix rules with a worked example, and the comparison table.
sem.oneIdea: The naive algorithm and why it is slow, the KMP failure function computed cell by cell with a full trace, Boyer–Moore's bad-character and good-suffix rules with a worked example, and the comparison table.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Compute the LPS / failure function for the given pattern” is the single most likely question here — it is short, mechanical, and worth 5 marks. Learn the table-building rule until it is automatic. Then “Search for the pattern in the text using KMP, showing all comparisons”. For Boyer–Moore, the bad-character rule is what gets examined; the good-suffix rule is usually only described. Learn the complexity comparison too — especially that Boyer–Moore can be sublinear, which surprises people.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Graph Representation, BFS and DFS
sem.deck: Adjacency matrix vs adjacency list, breadth-first search with a queue, depth-first search with a stack / recursion, edge classification — tree, back, forward, cross — and the time complexities that decide which to use.
sem.oneIdea: Adjacency matrix vs adjacency list, breadth-first search with a queue, depth-first search with a stack / recursion, edge classification — tree, back, forward, cross — and the time complexities that decide which to use.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Trace BFS / DFS on the given graph” is a guaranteed 5–10 marker. You must show the queue (BFS) or stack (DFS) contents at every step, the discovery/finish times for DFS, and the resulting tree. Know the O(V+E) complexity and when to use which.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Connected Components and Topological Sorting
sem.deck: Finding connected components in undirected graphs, strongly connected components (Kosaraju’s algorithm), topological sorting of DAGs by DFS reverse-finish and by Kahn’s BFS — with full worked traces.
sem.oneIdea: Finding connected components in undirected graphs, strongly connected components (Kosaraju’s algorithm), topological sorting of DAGs by DFS reverse-finish and by Kahn’s BFS — with full worked traces.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Find all connected components” is usually a sub-question. “Find a topological ordering of the given DAG” is a standalone 5–10 marker — show DFS with finish times, then list vertices in reverse finish order. Know Kahn’s algorithm too.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Biconnected Components and Articulation Points
sem.deck: Articulation points (cut vertices), bridges, biconnected components, and Tarjan’s DFS algorithm using low values — with a step-by-step worked trace.
sem.oneIdea: Articulation points (cut vertices), bridges, biconnected components, and Tarjan’s DFS algorithm using low values — with a step-by-step worked trace.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Find the articulation points and biconnected components” means: run DFS, compute low[] values, apply the two rules. Show the DFS tree with d[] and low[] at every node. This is a 5–10 marker.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Single-Source Shortest Path
sem.deck: Dijkstra’s algorithm for non-negative weights, Bellman–Ford for general weights with negative-cycle detection — both with full step-by-step worked traces.
sem.oneIdea: Dijkstra’s algorithm for non-negative weights, Bellman–Ford for general weights with negative-cycle detection — both with full step-by-step worked traces.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Apply Dijkstra’s algorithm on the given graph” is a guaranteed 10-mark numerical. Show the distance table and the vertex selected at each step. Know that Dijkstra fails with negative edges; Bellman–Ford handles them.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Greedy Method and Fractional Knapsack
sem.deck: The greedy-choice property and optimal substructure, when greedy works and when it doesn’t, and the fractional knapsack problem solved step by step.
sem.oneIdea: The greedy-choice property and optimal substructure, when greedy works and when it doesn’t, and the fractional knapsack problem solved step by step.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain greedy method with an example” is a guaranteed 5-marker. Fractional knapsack numerical is a common 5–10 mark problem — sort by value/weight ratio, fill greedily.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Minimum Spanning Trees — Prim’s and Kruskal’s
sem.deck: The MST problem, the cut property, Prim’s vertex-growing algorithm and Kruskal’s edge-sorting algorithm — both traced step by step — with time complexities and comparison.
sem.oneIdea: The MST problem, the cut property, Prim’s vertex-growing algorithm and Kruskal’s edge-sorting algorithm — both traced step by step — with time complexities and comparison.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Find MST using Prim’s / Kruskal’s” is a guaranteed 10-mark numerical. Show edges selected at each step, running weight, and the final MST weight. Know both algorithms and their complexities.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Huffman Coding
sem.deck: Prefix-free codes, building the Huffman tree using a priority queue, encoding and decoding, optimality of Huffman codes, and a complete worked example.
sem.oneIdea: Prefix-free codes, building the Huffman tree using a priority queue, encoding and decoding, optimality of Huffman codes, and a complete worked example.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Construct Huffman tree and codes for the given frequencies” is a guaranteed 10-marker. Show the priority queue at each merge step, draw the final tree, and list the codes.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Dynamic Programming — Matrix Chain Multiplication and Binomial Coefficient
sem.deck: The DP paradigm (overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure), the binomial coefficient table, and the matrix chain multiplication problem with a full table-filling trace.
sem.oneIdea: The DP paradigm (overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure), the binomial coefficient table, and the matrix chain multiplication problem with a full table-filling trace.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

MCM is a guaranteed 10–15 mark numerical. Fill the m[i][j] and s[i][j] tables. Show the formula, the chain length loop, and the final optimal parenthesisation. The binomial coefficient is a short 5-marker.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Dynamic Programming — LCS and 0/1 Knapsack
sem.deck: The Longest Common Subsequence problem and the 0/1 Knapsack problem — both with complete table-filling traces and backtracking to recover the solution.
sem.oneIdea: The Longest Common Subsequence problem and the 0/1 Knapsack problem — both with complete table-filling traces and backtracking to recover the solution.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Both LCS and 0/1 Knapsack are guaranteed 10-mark numericals. Fill the table, show the recurrence at each cell, and trace back to find the solution. These are the two most-examined DP problems.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: P, NP Classes and Non-Determinism
sem.deck: Decision vs optimization problems, deterministic vs non-deterministic algorithms, formal definitions of complexity classes P and NP, certificates and polynomial verifiers, and the P versus NP question.
sem.oneIdea: Decision vs optimization problems, deterministic vs non-deterministic algorithms, formal definitions of complexity classes P and NP, certificates and polynomial verifiers, and the P versus NP question.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Define Class P, Class NP, and Non-Deterministic algorithms with examples” is a standard 5-to-8 mark question. Distinguish clearly between solving an instance from scratch and verifying a proposed certificate.

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: NP-Completeness and Polynomial Reductions
sem.deck: Formal definitions of NP-Hard and NP-Complete, Euler/Venn complexity diagrams, polynomial-time reductions ($L_1 \le_P L_2$), transitivity, the 2-step NP-completeness proof recipe, and the Cook–Levin Theorem.
sem.oneIdea: Formal definitions of NP-Hard and NP-Complete, Euler/Venn complexity diagrams, polynomial-time reductions ($L_1 \le_P L_2$), transitivity, the 2-step NP-completeness proof recipe, and the Cook–Levin Theorem.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Define NP-Hard and NP-Complete” and “State the Cook-Levin Theorem and explain the steps to prove a problem is NP-Complete” are 10-mark examination essentials. Always draw the P vs NP Venn diagrams (both under $P \ne NP$ and $P = NP$).

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Classic NP-Complete Problems and Reductions
sem.deck: The grand tree of reductions: 3-SAT, the Clique decision problem, Vertex Cover, Set Cover, and step-by-step reduction gadget proofs.
sem.oneIdea: The grand tree of reductions: 3-SAT, the Clique decision problem, Vertex Cover, Set Cover, and step-by-step reduction gadget proofs.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Prove that the Clique Problem is NP-Complete by reducing from 3-SAT” and “Show that Vertex Cover is NP-Complete” are standard 10-mark examination proofs. Always write: (1) Certificate verification in polynomial time, (2) Gadget construction, and (3) Proof in both directions (if and only if).

sem.subject: Design & Analysis of Algorithms
sem.title: Hamiltonian Cycle, TSP and Approximations
sem.deck: Eulerian vs Hamiltonian graphs, Hamiltonian cycle NP-completeness, reducing Hamiltonian cycle to Traveling Salesman (TSP), and polynomial-time approximation algorithms.
sem.oneIdea: Eulerian vs Hamiltonian graphs, Hamiltonian cycle NP-completeness, reducing Hamiltonian cycle to Traveling Salesman (TSP), and polynomial-time approximation algorithms.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Prove that the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) is NP-Complete by reducing from Hamiltonian Cycle” is a guaranteed 7-to-10 mark question. “Explain the 2-approximation algorithm for Vertex Cover or Metric TSP” is the standard follow-up question.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: What Is Soft Computing
sem.deck: The definition, the four characteristics, and why the subject exists at all. Everything else in Unit I hangs off this page.
sem.oneIdea: The definition, the four characteristics, and why the subject exists at all. Everything else in Unit I hangs off this page.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

Almost every Unit I paper opens with "Define soft computing and state its importance" (2–5 marks). Zadeh's definition, quoted verbatim, is worth full marks on its own. Learn it word for word.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Hard vs Soft Computing
sem.deck: One table, eleven rows. This is the highest-probability question in the whole of Unit I — write it as a table, never as prose.
sem.oneIdea: One table, eleven rows. This is the highest-probability question in the whole of Unit I — write it as a table, never as prose.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Asked as "Compare hard and soft computing" (5–10 marks). Always answer in a table. A table of 8 rows scores higher than a page of paragraphs, takes a third of the time, and cannot be misread. Add one example row at the bottom and one closing line about hybrid systems.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: The Four Pillars
sem.deck: Fuzzy systems, rough sets, optimization and neural networks — what each one is for , in one paragraph each. Plus the applications list that closes Unit I.
sem.oneIdea: Fuzzy systems, rough sets, optimization and neural networks — what each one is for , in one paragraph each. Plus the applications list that closes Unit I.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

Your syllabus says "Overview of Fuzzy Systems, Rough Sets, Optimization, and Neural Networks". Overview is the operative word — Units II to V teach each one properly. Here you only need to say what each handles, who invented it, and what it is weak at. Do not over-write this in the exam.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Fuzzy Sets and Membership Functions
sem.deck: Partial membership, Zadeh's notation, the five standard membership functions, and the eight features (core, support, α-cut…) that every numerical question depends on.
sem.oneIdea: Partial membership, Zadeh's notation, the five standard membership functions, and the eight features (core, support, α-cut…) that every numerical question depends on.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

This lesson is the vocabulary for the entire unit. If you cannot state support, core, height and α-cut cold, you will lose marks in the defuzzification numericals too — the λ-cut method is literally an α-cut applied repeatedly.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Set Operations on Fuzzy Sets
sem.deck: Max, min, 1−μ — and the eight further operations built on them. Ends with the two classical laws that fuzzy sets break , which is a guaranteed exam question.
sem.oneIdea: Max, min, 1−μ — and the eight further operations built on them. Ends with the two classical laws that fuzzy sets break , which is a guaranteed exam question.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

The numerical "Given A and B, find union, intersection, complement, difference, algebraic sum and product" is close to certain to appear (5–10 marks). It is free marks — the arithmetic is trivial provided you have the formulas memorised exactly. Then the theory follow-up: "Which classical laws fail for fuzzy sets?"

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Fuzzy Relations and Composition
sem.deck: Cartesian product, the relation matrix, and max–min composition worked out cell by cell. This is the most reliably examined numerical in Unit II.
sem.oneIdea: Cartesian product, the relation matrix, and max–min composition worked out cell by cell. This is the most reliably examined numerical in Unit II.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

"Find R = A × B, then compute R ∘ S using max–min composition" is a 10-mark question that appears year after year. It is pure mechanics — if you can do the matrix drill you cannot lose the marks. Do the worked example below with a pen before you sleep.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Fuzzy If-Then Rules and Reasoning
sem.deck: Linguistic variables, hedges, the four implication operators, and the compositional rule of inference — how a rule plus an observation produces a conclusion.
sem.oneIdea: Linguistic variables, hedges, the four implication operators, and the compositional rule of inference — how a rule plus an observation produces a conclusion.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

Two things are examined here: the definition set (linguistic variable, hedge, fuzzy proposition, implication) as short questions, and the GMP numerical (B′ = A′ ∘ R), which is just Lesson 6's composition wearing a different hat. Get the vocabulary right and the numerical is already done.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Fuzzification and Defuzzification
sem.deck: Crisp in, crisp out. Seven defuzzification methods with their formulas, and four fully worked numericals — centroid, weighted average, mean of maxima and centre of sums.
sem.oneIdea: Crisp in, crisp out. Seven defuzzification methods with their formulas, and four fully worked numericals — centroid, weighted average, mean of maxima and centre of sums.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

Defuzzification is the highest-yield numerical in Unit II. "Find the defuzzified value using the centroid method" is close to guaranteed. The arithmetic is one division — the marks are lost on setting up ∑μ·z correctly, so do the worked examples with a pen, not by reading.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Fuzzy Inference Systems
sem.deck: Mamdani, Sugeno and Tsukamoto — the same problem solved three ways, so you can see exactly where the three models diverge. Plus the block diagram and the comparison table.
sem.oneIdea: Mamdani, Sugeno and Tsukamoto — the same problem solved three ways, so you can see exactly where the three models diverge. Plus the block diagram and the comparison table.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

Two near-certain questions. (a) "Draw and explain the architecture of a fuzzy inference system" — the four-block diagram, 5 marks. (b) "Compare Mamdani and Sugeno models" — a table, 5–10 marks. The numerical is the harder version of the same thing.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Fuzzy C-Means and Applications
sem.deck: Soft clustering — the objective function, the two update equations, one full iteration worked out, and the applications list that closes Unit II.
sem.oneIdea: Soft clustering — the objective function, the two update equations, one full iteration worked out, and the applications list that closes Unit II.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

Two questions live here. (a) "Explain the FCM algorithm" — write the objective function, the two update equations and the five steps. (b) "Compare K-means and FCM" — a short table. The full numerical is long; examiners usually ask for one iteration, which is what is worked below.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Introduction to Rough Set Theory
sem.deck: Pawlak’s 1982 framework for handling indiscernibility in data — information systems, equivalence classes, and the idea that a concept can be approximated from below and above when the attributes cannot separate it precisely.
sem.oneIdea: Pawlak’s 1982 framework for handling indiscernibility in data — information systems, equivalence classes, and the idea that a concept can be approximated from below and above when the attributes cannot separate it precisely.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

Unit III is the second pillar of soft computing after fuzzy sets. Examiners test whether you can state the formal definitions (information system, indiscernibility relation, approximations) and whether you know the fuzzy–rough distinction. This lesson sets up the vocabulary; Lessons 12–13 add the calculations.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Approximations and Boundary Region
sem.deck: Lower approximation, upper approximation, boundary region, negative region, accuracy of approximation — the five concepts that turn rough set theory into a classification tool, with two full worked examples .
sem.oneIdea: Lower approximation, upper approximation, boundary region, negative region, accuracy of approximation — the five concepts that turn rough set theory into a classification tool, with two full worked examples .
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

This is where the marks are in Unit III. The examiner will give you a decision table and ask you to find the lower approximation, upper approximation, boundary region, and accuracy. Every step below is what you write on the answer sheet.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Attribute Reduction and Core
sem.deck: Dispensable and indispensable attributes, reducts, core, and the discernibility matrix — the rough-set method for feature selection , with a full worked example finding the reduct and core from a decision table.
sem.oneIdea: Dispensable and indispensable attributes, reducts, core, and the discernibility matrix — the rough-set method for feature selection , with a full worked example finding the reduct and core from a decision table.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

Attribute reduction is the most practically important topic in Unit III. The examiner will give you a small decision table and ask: which attributes are dispensable? What is the reduct? What is the core? This lesson teaches the method step by step.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Applications of Rough Sets
sem.deck: Feature selection, data mining, machine learning, decision rule extraction, and the comparison with other methods — how the theory from Lessons 11–13 translates to real-world use.
sem.oneIdea: Feature selection, data mining, machine learning, decision rule extraction, and the comparison with other methods — how the theory from Lessons 11–13 translates to real-world use.
sem.keyVisual:
Why this matters tomorrow

The syllabus explicitly names feature selection, data mining, and machine learning as application areas. Expect a 5–10 mark question asking you to explain how rough sets are used in one or more of these. Structure your answer by application, not by theory.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Biological Neurons, Mathematical Models and ANN Architecture
sem.deck: The biological neuron (dendrites, soma, axon), McCulloch-Pitts model, activation functions (step, sigmoid, ReLU, tanh), single-layer and multi-layer network architectures, and how an artificial neuron computes.
sem.oneIdea: The biological neuron (dendrites, soma, axon), McCulloch-Pitts model, activation functions (step, sigmoid, ReLU, tanh), single-layer and multi-layer network architectures, and how an artificial neuron computes.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Draw and explain the mathematical model of a neuron” is a guaranteed 5-marker. Know the diagram (inputs, weights, summation, activation function, output) and at least three activation functions with their formulas and ranges.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Learning Rules and Paradigms
sem.deck: Three learning paradigms (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement), Hebbian learning rule, the delta rule (Widrow-Hoff / LMS), and the gradient descent idea that leads to back-propagation.
sem.oneIdea: Three learning paradigms (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement), Hebbian learning rule, the delta rule (Widrow-Hoff / LMS), and the gradient descent idea that leads to back-propagation.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Differentiate supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning” is a guaranteed short-answer. Hebbian rule and delta rule formulas are often asked as definitions.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Perceptron Training and Delta Rule
sem.deck: The single-layer perceptron, the perceptron learning algorithm with a full worked AND-gate example, the perceptron convergence theorem, XOR limitation, and why multi-layer networks are needed.
sem.oneIdea: The single-layer perceptron, the perceptron learning algorithm with a full worked AND-gate example, the perceptron convergence theorem, XOR limitation, and why multi-layer networks are needed.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Perceptron training numerical is a guaranteed 10-marker. Show weight updates epoch by epoch until convergence. “Why can’t a perceptron learn XOR?” is a classic short-answer.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Back-Propagation Algorithm
sem.deck: The MLP architecture, forward pass, error computation, backward pass (chain rule to compute gradients), weight update, and a simplified worked numerical for a 2-2-1 network.
sem.oneIdea: The MLP architecture, forward pass, error computation, backward pass (chain rule to compute gradients), weight update, and a simplified worked numerical for a 2-2-1 network.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Back-propagation numerical is a guaranteed 15-mark question. Given a small network with initial weights and one training sample, show: forward pass (compute outputs), error, backward pass (compute δ for output and hidden layers), weight updates. Use the sigmoid and its derivative f′(x) = f(x)(1 − f(x)).

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Hopfield Networks, Associative Memories and Applications
sem.deck: Hopfield network architecture, energy function and convergence, auto-associative and hetero-associative memories, and neural network applications in pattern recognition, forecasting, and image processing.
sem.oneIdea: Hopfield network architecture, energy function and convergence, auto-associative and hetero-associative memories, and neural network applications in pattern recognition, forecasting, and image processing.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain Hopfield network with energy function” is a guaranteed question. Know: fully connected, symmetric weights (wij = wji), no self-connections, converges to local energy minimum. Applications are a common 5-marker list.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Genetic Algorithm Fundamentals
sem.deck: Biological roots, chromosome representations, fitness landscapes, selection mechanisms (Roulette Wheel, Tournament, Rank), crossover and mutation operators, and the canonical evolutionary cycle.
sem.oneIdea: Biological roots, chromosome representations, fitness landscapes, selection mechanisms (Roulette Wheel, Tournament, Rank), crossover and mutation operators, and the canonical evolutionary cycle.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain the working cycle of a Genetic Algorithm with a neat flowchart” and “Calculate selection probabilities using Roulette Wheel Selection” are recurrent 5-to-10 mark questions. Make sure you memorize the selection probability formula P_i = f_i / Σf_j, know at least three encoding techniques, and understand why elitism prevents loss of the best candidate solution.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: GA Worked Example and Multi-Objective GA
sem.deck: A complete step-by-step GA manual numerical (fitness evaluation, roulette wheel selection, single-point crossover, bit mutation), followed by Multi-Objective Optimization, Pareto dominance, and NSGA-II principles.
sem.oneIdea: A complete step-by-step GA manual numerical (fitness evaluation, roulette wheel selection, single-point crossover, bit mutation), followed by Multi-Objective Optimization, Pareto dominance, and NSGA-II principles.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Solve one complete generation of a Genetic Algorithm to maximize f(x) = x²” is a guaranteed 10-marker. University evaluators look for the exact table structure: chromosome string → decoded integer → fitness → selection probability → cumulative range → mating pool → crossover calculation → final generation comparison. For theory, Pareto dominance and NSGA-II non-dominated sorting are top-tier questions.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Particle Swarm Optimization
sem.deck: Kennedy & Eberhart's swarm intelligence model, velocity and position update equations, inertia weight dynamics, step-by-step worked numerical iteration, and a comprehensive PSO vs GA comparison.
sem.oneIdea: Kennedy & Eberhart's swarm intelligence model, velocity and position update equations, inertia weight dynamics, step-by-step worked numerical iteration, and a comprehensive PSO vs GA comparison.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“State the velocity and position update equations in PSO and explain each term” is a mandatory 5-mark question. You must describe the three velocity components: inertia term (momentum), cognitive term (personal memory), and social term (swarm cooperation). The PSO vs GA comparison table is equally popular as a 5-to-7 mark question.

sem.subject: Soft Computing
sem.title: Ant Colony Optimization & Real-World Applications
sem.deck: Marco Dorigo's stigmergic foraging model, transition probability rule, pheromone deposition and evaporation dynamics, complete worked graph numerical, GA vs PSO vs ACO comparison, and real-world optimization domains.
sem.oneIdea: Marco Dorigo's stigmergic foraging model, transition probability rule, pheromone deposition and evaporation dynamics, complete worked graph numerical, GA vs PSO vs ACO comparison, and real-world optimization domains.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“State and explain the state transition and pheromone update equations in ACO” is a top-probability 5-to-10 mark question. Always define the parameters clearly: α (pheromone weight), β (heuristic visibility weight), ρ (evaporation rate), and η = 1/d. The three-way comparison table (GA vs PSO vs ACO) and real-world applications are frequently paired to form a full 10-mark question.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Message Integrity
sem.deck: Why encryption alone is not enough, what a message digest is, and the document-and-fingerprint model that every later topic in this unit is built on.
sem.oneIdea: Why encryption alone is not enough, what a message digest is, and the document-and-fingerprint model that every later topic in this unit is built on.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

This lesson is the opening paragraph of almost every long answer in Unit I. Two questions come straight from it: “What is message integrity? Explain with the document and fingerprint analogy” and “Distinguish between confidentiality, integrity, authentication and non-repudiation.” Write the four-goal table first, then narrow to integrity — examiners reward the framing, not just the definition.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Hash Functions and Their Properties
sem.deck: The three resistance properties, the requirements list, the Merkle–Damgård iterated structure that MD4, SHA-512 and Whirlpool all share, and the applications. The most reliably asked topic in Unit I.
sem.oneIdea: The three resistance properties, the requirements list, the Merkle–Damgård iterated structure that MD4, SHA-512 and Whirlpool all share, and the applications. The most reliably asked topic in Unit I.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three questions, and one of them is close to certain: “What is a cryptographic hash function? Explain its properties.” Answer it with the three resistance properties named and defined — preimage, second preimage, collision — not with a vague list of adjectives. The other two: “Explain the iterated (Merkle–Damgård) hash function structure” with the diagram, and “Differentiate hashing from encryption.”

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: The Random Oracle Model
sem.deck: The ideal hash function that real hash functions are measured against — how the oracle behaves, the birthday problems that follow from it, the three attacks on hash functions, and why 512-bit digests exist.
sem.oneIdea: The ideal hash function that real hash functions are measured against — how the oracle behaves, the birthday problems that follow from it, the three attacks on hash functions, and why 512-bit digests exist.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

A short-note or 5-mark question, almost always phrased “Explain the Random Oracle Model” or “What is an ideal hash function?” The full marks come from three things: the oracle’s three rules, the “it is a theoretical model, no real function achieves it” caveat, and the birthday attack bound 2n/2 that comes out of it. It is also the topic students skip, which makes it cheap marks.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Message Authentication: MAC, HMAC and CMAC
sem.deck: Adding a secret key to the digest so it can travel the insecure channel — the MAC and its security requirements, the nested construction HMAC with its ipad and opad, and the block-cipher construction CMAC with its two subkeys.
sem.oneIdea: Adding a secret key to the digest so it can travel the insecure channel — the MAC and its security requirements, the nested construction HMAC with its ipad and opad, and the block-cipher construction CMAC with its two subkeys.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

The highest-yield lesson in Unit I — expect a full 10-mark question. The three that recur: “What is a MAC? Explain message authentication with a diagram”, “Explain HMAC with its block diagram” (the ipad/opad formula is the mark-earner), and “Differentiate HMAC and CMAC” or “MAC vs MDC vs digital signature”. Always finish a MAC answer with the sentence “a MAC gives integrity and authentication but not non-repudiation, because the key is shared.”

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: MD4 — Message Digest 4
sem.deck: The 128-bit digest, the 512-bit block, the four-word buffer, three rounds of sixteen steps, and the three boolean functions. The ancestor of MD5, SHA-1 and RIPEMD, and the reason all of them look alike.
sem.oneIdea: The 128-bit digest, the 512-bit block, the four-word buffer, three rounds of sixteen steps, and the three boolean functions. The ancestor of MD5, SHA-1 and RIPEMD, and the reason all of them look alike.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Asked as “Explain the MD4 algorithm” or, very often, “Explain MD5 / the MD family” — the two are close enough that one answer with a comparison table covers both. Marks sit in the parameter table (128 / 512 / 3 rounds / 48 steps), the padding rule, the three round functions and the diagram of one step. Do not try to memorise the shift amounts or the message-word order; no examiner asks for them.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: SHA-512
sem.deck: The SHA family table, the five steps, the 1024-bit block and 80 rounds, the word-expansion schedule, the six logical functions — and the padding numerical, the one calculation this unit sets.
sem.oneIdea: The SHA family table, the five steps, the 1024-bit block and 80 rounds, the word-expansion schedule, the six logical functions — and the padding numerical, the one calculation this unit sets.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

The single most likely long question in Unit I: “Explain the SHA-512 algorithm with a block diagram.” Structure the answer as parameters table → five steps → round function → word expansion, and draw two diagrams: the overall Merkle–Damgård chain and one round with the eight registers. The padding numerical is a near-certain 2–5 mark sub-question — it takes thirty seconds once the rule is memorised, so never leave it.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Whirlpool
sem.deck: The 512-bit hash built from a block cipher instead of from scratch — the Miyaguchi–Preneel scheme, the AES-like cipher W with its four round transformations, and the three-way comparison that closes Unit I.
sem.oneIdea: The 512-bit hash built from a block cipher instead of from scratch — the Miyaguchi–Preneel scheme, the AES-like cipher W with its four round transformations, and the three-way comparison that closes Unit I.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Usually a 5-mark short note: “Explain the Whirlpool hash function.” The marks are in four facts — 512-bit digest from a 512-bit block cipher W, the Miyaguchi–Preneel equation, 10 rounds of four AES-like transformations, and designed by Rijmen and Barreto, an ISO standard. If a longer question asks to compare MD5, SHA-512 and Whirlpool, the table at the end of this lesson is the answer in full.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Elliptic Curve Cryptography — the Arithmetic
sem.deck: The curve equation, the group law, point addition and doubling over Z p with every step shown, finding all points on a curve, scalar multiplication by double-and-add, and the ECDLP that makes it hard.
sem.oneIdea: The curve equation, the group law, point addition and doubling over Z p with every step shown, finding all points on a curve, scalar multiplication by double-and-add, and the ECDLP that makes it hard.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

This is a numerical lesson — treat it like subnetting, not like theory. Three question shapes recur: “Find all points on the curve Ep(a,b)”, “Given P and Q on the curve, find P+Q and 2P”, and “Compute kP”. Learn the two λ formulas and the fact that division means multiply by the modular inverse; everything else follows mechanically. Write the formula before substituting — that alone carries marks even if the arithmetic slips.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: ECC Cryptosystems — ECDH and EC ElGamal
sem.deck: Turning the point arithmetic into cryptography: key generation, Diffie–Hellman key exchange on a curve, elliptic curve ElGamal encryption and decryption — both worked end to end — plus the ECC-versus-RSA argument.
sem.oneIdea: Turning the point arithmetic into cryptography: key generation, Diffie–Hellman key exchange on a curve, elliptic curve ElGamal encryption and decryption — both worked end to end — plus the ECC-versus-RSA argument.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Two numericals and one table. “Perform ECDH key exchange on the given curve” and “Encrypt and decrypt the message point using EC ElGamal” are both mechanical once Lesson 8 is solid — the whole difficulty is the point arithmetic, not the protocol. The table is “Compare ECC with RSA”, worth memorising because it also answers “advantages of ECC”.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Digital Signature
sem.deck: The process, the properties a signature must have, why the digest is signed rather than the message, direct versus arbitrated signatures, and the comparison tables against MAC and against a handwritten signature.
sem.oneIdea: The process, the properties a signature must have, why the digest is signed rather than the message, direct versus arbitrated signatures, and the comparison tables against MAC and against a handwritten signature.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Near-certain 10-mark question: “What is a digital signature? Explain the signing and verification process with a diagram.” The diagram carries half the marks — draw hash → encrypt with private key → send M + signature → hash again, decrypt with public key, compare. Add the three services (authentication, integrity, non-repudiation) and the sentence “signing gives no confidentiality unless the message is separately encrypted”. The MAC-versus-signature table is the standard follow-up.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Attacks on Digital Signatures
sem.deck: What the adversary is allowed to do, the four levels of success, and the specific attacks — existential forgery, the multiplicative property, blinding, birthday and replay — three of them worked with real numbers.
sem.oneIdea: What the adversary is allowed to do, the four levels of success, and the specific attacks — existential forgery, the multiplicative property, blinding, birthday and replay — three of them worked with real numbers.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Asked as “Explain the attacks on digital signatures”, usually 5–10 marks. Answer in two lists, not one: first the attack types (what the attacker can obtain), then the forgery levels (what counts as a break). Then give two or three concrete attacks with their countermeasures. That structure is what separates a full-mark answer from a list of half-remembered names.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: RSA and ElGamal Digital Signature Schemes
sem.deck: The two founding schemes, each worked end to end with numbers — key generation, signing, verification, and the algebra that proves the verification works. Plus the nonce-reuse attack that recovers ElGamal’s private key, worked in full.
sem.oneIdea: The two founding schemes, each worked end to end with numbers — key generation, signing, verification, and the algebra that proves the verification works. Plus the nonce-reuse attack that recovers ElGamal’s private key, worked in full.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Both schemes are guaranteed numericals. RSA signing is the easier of the two and is often a 5-mark sub-question; ElGamal is a full 10-mark question because it has more moving parts. Always write the formula, then substitute, then check the verification condition — a verification that comes out equal is your own proof that the arithmetic is right. Learn the ElGamal verification equation αM ≡ yrrs as a unit; it is the line most often forgotten.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Schnorr and the Digital Signature Standard
sem.deck: The two schemes that shrink ElGamal by working in a small subgroup of order q — Schnorr with its precomputation trick, DSA with its two-modulus structure — each worked end to end with numbers.
sem.oneIdea: The two schemes that shrink ElGamal by working in a small subgroup of order q — Schnorr with its precomputation trick, DSA with its two-modulus structure — each worked end to end with numbers.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

DSS is the more likely of the two to appear as a full 10-mark numerical; Schnorr is usually 5 marks or a comparison. For DSA, memorise the five signing values (p, q, g, x, y) and the two-line signature (r, s), and above all the verification chain w → u1 → u2 → v. The examiner’s favourite one-liner is “why are r and s reduced mod q?” — because it makes the signature 320 bits instead of 2048.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: ECDSA, Variations and Applications
sem.deck: DSA moved onto an elliptic curve, worked end to end on a real curve; the five-scheme comparison table that closes the unit; and the variations — blind, proxy, group, ring, undeniable, multi-signature — with where signatures are actually used.
sem.oneIdea: DSA moved onto an elliptic curve, worked end to end on a real curve; the five-scheme comparison table that closes the unit; and the variations — blind, proxy, group, ring, undeniable, multi-signature — with where signatures are actually used.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Three separate marks-earners here. ECDSA is a numerical, and it is just DSA with point multiplication in place of exponentiation — if DSA is solid, this is nearly free. “Variations of digital signatures” is a definitional 5-marker where one line per variation plus its application is exactly what is wanted. “Applications of digital signatures” is the easiest question in the unit — but only if you have a list ready, so learn six.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Entity Authentication and Passwords
sem.deck: The difference between message authentication and entity authentication, the three factor categories, password-based schemes — fixed passwords, one-time passwords (OTP), S/Key and the dictionary attack — and why passwords alone are never enough.
sem.oneIdea: The difference between message authentication and entity authentication, the three factor categories, password-based schemes — fixed passwords, one-time passwords (OTP), S/Key and the dictionary attack — and why passwords alone are never enough.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Entity authentication vs message authentication is a guaranteed 2–4 marker. Password attacks (dictionary, brute-force, replay) and countermeasures (salting, hashing, OTP) are a separate 5-marker. This lesson covers both.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Challenge-Response and Zero-Knowledge Protocols
sem.deck: Nonce-based authentication, symmetric and asymmetric challenge-response, the Needham–Schroeder flaw, and zero-knowledge proofs — proving you know a secret without revealing it.
sem.oneIdea: Nonce-based authentication, symmetric and asymmetric challenge-response, the Needham–Schroeder flaw, and zero-knowledge proofs — proving you know a secret without revealing it.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Challenge-response is a 5–10 mark question asking you to draw the protocol and explain how it defeats replay attacks. Zero-knowledge proofs are tested as definitions with the cave analogy or the Fiat–Shamir protocol. Know both.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Biometrics
sem.deck: “Something you are” — physiological and behavioural biometrics, the enrollment-verification pipeline, FAR vs FRR, the seven biometric types, and why biometrics alone are insufficient.
sem.oneIdea: “Something you are” — physiological and behavioural biometrics, the enrollment-verification pipeline, FAR vs FRR, the seven biometric types, and why biometrics alone are insufficient.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

This is a short-note or comparison-table question. Know: the seven types, the FAR/FRR/EER definitions, the enrollment-verification process, and advantages vs disadvantages. A table scores better than prose.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Symmetric-Key Distribution and Kerberos
sem.deck: The key distribution problem, KDCs, the Needham–Schroeder protocol, Kerberos v5 with its three exchanges, and Diffie–Hellman key agreement — the two ways to establish a shared key.
sem.oneIdea: The key distribution problem, KDCs, the Needham–Schroeder protocol, Kerberos v5 with its three exchanges, and Diffie–Hellman key agreement — the two ways to establish a shared key.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Kerberos is a guaranteed 10-marker — draw the three exchanges (AS, TGS, application), label every message, and name the tickets. Diffie–Hellman may appear here or in Unit IV. Know the man-in-the-middle attack on DH.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Public-Key Distribution and Hijacking
sem.deck: How public keys are distributed securely — public announcement, directory, CA and certificates, X.509 — and the attacks that exploit weak distribution: man-in-the-middle, session hijacking, and certificate spoofing.
sem.oneIdea: How public keys are distributed securely — public announcement, directory, CA and certificates, X.509 — and the attacks that exploit weak distribution: man-in-the-middle, session hijacking, and certificate spoofing.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

Four methods of public-key distribution is a guaranteed question — present as a table with advantages and weaknesses. Hijacking is tested as “explain session hijacking with diagram” or as a part of MITM.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: Email Security — PGP and S/MIME
sem.deck: Why email needs security, Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) services and message format, the web of trust, S/MIME and its use of certificates, and how PGP and S/MIME compare.
sem.oneIdea: Why email needs security, Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) services and message format, the web of trust, S/MIME and its use of certificates, and how PGP and S/MIME compare.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain PGP services and message format” is a guaranteed question. Know the five services (confidentiality, authentication, compression, compatibility, segmentation) and the order of operations. PGP vs S/MIME comparison is a common short-note.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: SSL and TLS
sem.deck: The SSL/TLS protocol stack, the handshake protocol step by step, record protocol, session vs connection, TLS 1.2 vs 1.3 differences, and how HTTPS works.
sem.oneIdea: The SSL/TLS protocol stack, the handshake protocol step by step, record protocol, session vs connection, TLS 1.2 vs 1.3 differences, and how HTTPS works.
sem.keyVisual:
Exam strategy

“Explain SSL/TLS handshake protocol” is a guaranteed 10-marker. Draw the message exchange (ClientHello, ServerHello, Certificate, KeyExchange, ChangeCipherSpec, Finished). Know the four protocols in the SSL stack.

sem.subject: Info & Data Security
sem.title: IPSec — AH, ESP and Modes
sem.deck: IP Security at the network layer, the two modes (transport and tunnel), the two security protocols (AH and ESP), what each protects, and how they compare.
